For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: For each $n\ge M$, [F1] and [F2] give $$\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\frac{dt}{t}-\frac1{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\left(\frac1t-\frac1{n+1}\right)dt.$$ The integrand is nonnegative and at most $1/n-1/(n+1)$ on this interval. Therefore $$0\le\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1}\le\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}.$$

Summing step 1.1 for $n=M,\ldots,K$ telescopes to $$0\le\gamma_M-\gamma_{K+1}\le\frac1M-\frac1{K+1}.$$ Let $K\to\infty$ and use $\gamma_{K+1}\to\gamma$ from [F1]. Since $\gamma_M=H_M-\log M$, the claimed two-sided bound follows.

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,$$

where for $t>0$ one uses the real logarithm convention
$t^{z-1}:=\exp((z-1)\log t)$.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the
displayed domain.

The improper integral

$$\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$$

converges locally uniformly on $\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$.

Euler's Gamma function is holomorphic on the half-plane
$\operatorname{Re}z>0$.

For every $z$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$,

$$\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z).$$
In a Dedekind-complete ordered field, the natural numbers are unbounded above.

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge0$, let $V_m=\{w\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}w>-m-1\}$ and define $G_m(w)=\Gamma(w+m+1)/(w(w+1)\cdots(w+m))$ as a meromorphic function on $V_m$. Its numerator is holomorphic on this half-plane by [F1] and [F2], and its denominator is a polynomial.

For every $w\in V_m$, $\operatorname{Re}(w+m+1)>0$. Applying [F3] at $w+m+1$ and cancelling the common meromorphic factor $w+m+1$ gives $G_{m+1}(w)=G_m(w)$ on the overlap $V_m\subset V_{m+1}$. By [F4], the union of the $V_m$ is $\mathbb C$, so these compatible meromorphic formulas define a meromorphic continuation of Euler's Gamma function on the whole plane.

Choose $m\ge1$ large enough that $z\in V_m$; then $z+1\in V_{m-1}$. Because $z$ is not a nonpositive integer, the denominator factors below are nonzero. The glued formulas give $\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+m+1)/(z(z+1)\cdots(z+m))$ and $\Gamma(z+1)=\Gamma(z+m+1)/((z+1)\cdots(z+m))$. Multiplying the first identity by $z$ yields the second.

For $T_k=c_kz^k$ with $c_k\ne0$, $|T_{k+3}|/|T_k|=|z|^3/((k+3)(k+2))$. This tends to zero and decreases in $k$; once all subsequent ratios are at most $q<1$, summing the geometric majorant gives $\sum_{j\ge0}|T_{k_0+3j}|\le|T_{k_0}|/(1-q)$.

On every disk $|z|\le R$, the ratios of each residue-class term and of its first two formal derivative series tend to zero uniformly as $k\to\infty$. Applying the geometric bound from step 1.2 to each class gives locally uniform convergence of the series and differentiated series. The series have infinite radius by these bounds, so [F2] permits termwise differentiation; step 1.1 then proves the Airy equation for the sums.

citations.quote:
For $z\in\mathbb C$, define the Fresnel functions and error function by

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
If $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: Dividing successive absolute terms in [F1] gives the stated ratio. For $k\ge K+1$ it is at most $q<1$, so the tail is dominated by $|e_{K+1}|\sum_{j\ge0}q^j=|e_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. On every disk the ratio is eventually below $1$, proving local uniform convergence.

The series in [F1] has infinite radius by step 1.1, so [F3] gives $$\operatorname{erf}'(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k}}{k!}=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\exp(-z^2),$$ using [F2] and the definition of the exponential series. Thus erf is an entire primitive of the stated integrand and $\operatorname{erf}(0)=0$.

Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb C$ be any piecewise continuously differentiable path with $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma(1)=z$. On a smooth piece, put $\eta_h=\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)$. Complex differentiability gives $\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s)+\eta_h)-\operatorname{erf}(\gamma(s)) =\operatorname{erf}'(\gamma(s))\eta_h+\eta_h\epsilon(\eta_h)$ with $\epsilon(\eta)\to0$ as $\eta\to0$; take $\epsilon(0)=0$. Since $\eta_h/h\to\gamma'(s)$, division by $h$ makes the remainder tend to zero and proves $(\operatorname{erf}\circ\gamma)'(s)=\operatorname{erf}'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. The derivative is continuous on that compact piece and its real and imaginary parts are integrable by [F4]. Applying [F4] componentwise and adding over the finitely many pieces gives $$\int_{\gamma}\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}e^{-t^2}\,dt=\operatorname{erf}(z)-\operatorname{erf}(0)=\operatorname{erf}(z).$$ This proves the segment identity and path independence without interchanging a series limit with a line integral.

derivations.claim: Taking ratios in [F1] gives $$\frac{|c_{k+1}|}{|c_k|}=\frac{\pi^2|z|^4}{4} \frac{4k+1}{(2k+1)(2k+2)(4k+5)},\qquad \frac{|s_{k+1}|}{|s_k|}=\frac{\pi^2|z|^4}{4} \frac{4k+3}{(2k+2)(2k+3)(4k+7)}.$$ The omitted factors are each less than $1$, yielding the displayed bounds.
The denominators in the bounds grow quadratically in $k$, so the ratios tend to zero; summing the resulting geometric majorant gives the stated tail bound and uniform convergence on every disk.

The infinite-radius power series in [F1] may be differentiated termwise by [F3]. The resulting derivatives are $$C'(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k}}{(2k)!}=\cos(\pi z^2/2),\qquad S'(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+2}}{(2k+1)!}=\sin(\pi z^2/2),$$ where the last equalities use [F2].

Both $C$ and $S$ are entire primitives of their displayed integrands. For any piecewise continuously differentiable path $\gamma$ from $0$ to $z$, put $\eta_h=\gamma(s+h)-\gamma(s)$ on each smooth piece. Complex differentiability gives $C(\gamma(s)+\eta_h)-C(\gamma(s))=C'(\gamma(s))\eta_h+ \eta_h\epsilon_C(\eta_h)$ with $\epsilon_C(\eta)\to0$ as $\eta\to0$; take $\epsilon_C(0)=0$. Since $\eta_h/h\to\gamma'(s)$, division by $h$ makes the remainder tend to zero, and hence $(C\circ\gamma)'(s)=C'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. The same calculation gives $(S\circ\gamma)'(s)=S'(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)$. These derivatives are continuous on compact path pieces and integrable by [F4]. The componentwise fundamental theorem and finite additivity therefore give the endpoint differences $C(z)-C(0)=C(z)$ and $S(z)-S(0)=S(z)$. Hence the integrals are path-independent and, in particular, equal the integrals along the segment from $0$ to $z$.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

derivations.claim: For either term sequence, cancellation of the factorials gives $|a_{k+1}|/|a_k|=|z|^2/[4(k+1)(k+n+1)]$ whenever $a_k\ne0$; at $z=0$ the series are finite-valued directly. This ratio decreases to $0$.

For $k\ge K+1$ the ratios are at most $q$, so $\sum_{k=K+1}^{\infty}|a_k|\le |a_{K+1}|\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^j =|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. On every disk $|z|\le R$, the ratio is bounded by the same expression with $R$ in place of $|z|$, which is eventually below $1$; the Weierstrass test gives uniform convergence there.

A derivative of order $d\in\{1,2\}$ multiplies the $k$th monomial by a factor bounded by $(2k+n)^d$ and lowers its power by $d$. The ratio of successive absolute differentiated terms is therefore $r_k$ times a factor that tends to $1$; on each disk it is eventually bounded by a constant below $1$. Thus both differentiated series converge uniformly on compact disks and may be differentiated termwise.

For complex parameters $p,q$ with $\operatorname{Re}p>0$ and
$\operatorname{Re}q>0$, define Euler's Beta function by

$$B(p,q):=\int_0^1 t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt,$$

again using the real logarithm on $(0,1)$ to define the complex powers.

The Beta-Gamma theorem below justifies convergence on exactly this pair of right
half-planes.

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,$$

where for $t>0$ one uses the real logarithm convention
$t^{z-1}:=\exp((z-1)\log t)$.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the
displayed domain.

The improper integral

$$\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$$

converges locally uniformly on $\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$.

The **Euler-Mascheroni constant** is

$$ \gamma:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n-\log N\right), $$

provided the limit exists.

For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on
$(a,b)$, with $a<b$. Then there is $c\in(a,b)$ such that
$$
f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a).
$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

derivations.claim: For $w=z/n$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the path $1+tw$ lies in the principal-logarithm domain. Its derivative integrand is continuous on $[0,1]$ and is integrable by [F3]. By [F2], [F3], and the real-parameter chain rule, $$\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{w}{1+tw}\,dt,\qquad w-\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{tw^2}{1+tw}\,dt.$$ Since $|1+tw|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}w+t^2|w|^2\ge1$, the summand has absolute value at most $|z|^2/(2n^2)$. Summing this bound is uniform on every compact subset of the right half-plane. Each summand is holomorphic there, so the series converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function by [F11].

For $N\ge1$, the Beta integrals satisfy $$B(z,1)=\frac1z,\qquad B(z,N+1)=\frac{N}{z+N}B(z,N).$$ For the base formula, apply [F3] componentwise on $[\varepsilon,1]$ to the primitive $t^z/z$ and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$; the lower boundary tends to $0$ since $|\varepsilon^z|=\varepsilon^{\operatorname{Re}z}$. For $N\ge1$, differentiate $g(t)=t^z(1-t)^N$ on $[\varepsilon,1]$. By [F6], $$g'(t)=zt^{z-1}(1-t)^N-Nt^z(1-t)^{N-1}.$$ The derivative is continuous and integrable on this compact interval by [F3]. Applying the componentwise fundamental theorem and then letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $zB(z,N+1)=NB(z+1,N)$; both boundary terms vanish. The integrand identity $t^{z-1}(1-t)^{N-1}=t^{z-1}(1-t)^N+t^z(1-t)^{N-1}$ and [F4] give $B(z,N)=B(z,N+1)+B(z+1,N)$. Combining these two equalities yields $(z+N)B(z,N+1)=NB(z,N)$, proving the recurrence. Iterating it from $B(z,1)=1/z$ gives $$B(z,N+1)=\frac{N!}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+N)}.$$ All denominators are nonzero because $\operatorname{Re}(z+j)>0$ for $j\ge0$.

Fix $z$ with $a:=\operatorname{Re}z>0$, and define $K_N(u)=(1-u/N)^N$ for $0\le u\le N$ and $K_N(u)=0$ for $u>N$. For $0\le u<N$, [F5] and [F12] give $$\log(1-u/N)=-\int_0^{u/N}\frac{ds}{1-s}\le-\frac{u}{N},$$ so $0\le K_N(u)\le e^{-u}$ by exponential monotonicity and the addition law; the same bound holds at $u=N$. On a fixed interval $[0,R]$, for $N>2R$, $$N\log(1-u/N)=-u-\delta_N(u),\qquad 0\le\delta_N(u)=N\int_0^{u/N}\frac{s}{1-s}\,ds\le\frac{R^2}{N}.$$ The mean value theorem in [F10] and $e^t\le1$ for $t\le0$ give $|K_N(u)-e^{-u}|\le R^2/N$ uniformly on $[0,R]$.

Define $$A_N(z):=\frac{N!\,N^z}{z(z+1)\cdots(z+N)},\qquad N^z:=\exp(z\log N).$$ By step 1.2 and the substitution $u=Nt$ in [F12], $$A_N(z)=N^zB(z,N+1) =\int_0^N u^{z-1}\left(1-\frac{u}{N}\right)^Ndu.$$ The real logarithm laws in [F5] preserve the stated power convention under this substitution.

By [F7], $|u^{z-1}|=u^{a-1}$. For each real or imaginary component, the integral difference on $[0,R]$ is bounded, using [F4], by $$\frac{R^2}{N}\int_0^R u^{a-1}\,du=\frac{R^{a+2}}{aN}.$$ On $[R,\infty)$, $K_N(u)\le e^{-u}$ bounds the difference in each component by $2\int_R^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}\,du$, which tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$ by [F8]. First choosing $R$ large and then $N$ large proves $A_N(z)\to\Gamma(z)$.

Let $\ell_N(z)$ be the defining partial sum through $N$ and put $$P_N(z):=z\exp(\gamma_E z)\prod_{n=1}^N\left(1+\frac zn\right)e^{-z/n}.$$ The principal-log identity $\exp(\operatorname{Log}w)=w$, the exponential addition law in [F6], and the formula from step 1.2 give $$\exp(\ell_N(z))=P_N(z)^{-1},\qquad P_N(z)A_N(z)=\exp\!\left(z(\gamma_E+\log N-H_N)\right).$$ By [F9] the second expression tends to $1$. By step 1.1, $\ell_N(z)\to\ell_+(z)$; continuity of the complex exponential gives $P_N(z)\to\exp(-\ell_+(z))$. Step 2.2 gives $A_N(z)\to\Gamma(z)$, so $$\exp(-\ell_+(z))\Gamma(z)=1.$$ Multiplying by $\exp(\ell_+(z))$ and using the addition law proves $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$.

finite_smoke.asserts:
- For $C$, sum its defining terms $c_0,\ldots,c_{q-1}$ from
  [[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]] by interval arithmetic,
  using $P_q/2$ for $\pi/2$. Let $c_q$ be the first omitted term and set
  $$r_C=\frac{(\sup P_q)^2 M(z)^4}{4(2q+1)(2q+2)}.$$
  If $r_C<1$, enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both coordinates by
  $M(c_q)/(1-r_C)$; otherwise skip this stage.
- For $S$, sum its first $q$ defining terms using $P_q/2$, let $s_q$
  be the first omitted term, and set
  $$r_S=\frac{(\sup P_q)^2 M(z)^4}{4(2q+2)(2q+3)}.$$
  If $r_S<1$, enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both coordinates by
  $M(s_q)/(1-r_S)$; otherwise skip this stage.
- For erf, use the interval $2/R_q$ from the single square-root call above
  for $2/\sqrt\pi$,
  sum the first $q$ defining terms, and let $e_q$ be the first omitted
  term. Set $r_E=M(z)^2/(q+1)$. If $r_E<1$, enlarge the partial-sum
  rectangle in both coordinates by $M(e_q)/(1-r_E)$; otherwise skip this
  stage.
- For the Gauss series, compute its terms by $h_0=1$ and
  $$h_{k+1}=h_k\,z\,\frac{(a+k)(b+k)}{(c+k)(k+1)}$$
  using exact interval operations. No denominator $c+k$ vanishes by the
  domain check. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, let $L$ be one
  more than the smaller absolute value of those nonpositive integer
  parameters. If $L\le q$, sum exactly through $h_{L-1}$ and use zero
  tail. Otherwise put
  $$A=|\Re a|+|\Im a|,\quad B=|\Re b|+|\Im b|,\quad C_0=|\Re c|+|\Im c|,\quad Z_0=|\Re z|+|\Im z|,$$
  and
  $$r_H=Z_0\frac{(1+A/q)(1+B/q)}{1-C_0/q}.$$
  If $q>C_0$ and $r_H<1$, sum $h_0,\ldots,h_{q-1}$, let $h_q$
  be the first omitted term, and enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both
  coordinates by $M(h_q)/(1-r_H)$; otherwise skip this stage. The geometric
  bound in [[lem-gauss-hypergeometric-series-geometric-tail]] applies because
  $A,B,C_0,Z_0$ dominate the corresponding complex moduli.

citations.quote:
The coefficient recurrence in [[def-airy-initial-value-series]] makes both
series solve $y''=zy$. In a residue class $k\equiv r\pmod 3$, successive
nonzero terms have absolute ratio

$$\frac{|z|^3}{(k+3)(k+2)}.$$

If the ratio of each term after a chosen first omitted term is bounded by
$q<1$, that class's tail is at most the first omitted term's absolute value
divided by $1-q$. The series and their first two derivative series converge
locally uniformly on $\mathbb C$.

For $y(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}c_kz^k$, set $c_2=0$ and
$c_{k+3}=c_k/((k+3)(k+2))$ for $k\ge0$. Define $\operatorname{Ai}$ by this
series with

$$c_0=\frac{1}{3^{2/3}\Gamma(2/3)},\qquad c_1=-\frac{1}{3^{1/3}\Gamma(1/3)},$$

and define $\operatorname{Bi}$ by the same recurrence with

$$c_0=\frac{1}{3^{1/6}\Gamma(2/3)},\qquad c_1=\frac{3^{1/6}}{\Gamma(1/3)}.$$

Here $\Gamma$ is Euler's integral on the right half-plane from
[[def-euler-gamma-function]]. The standard Airy initial values are those in
DLMF §9.2(ii); in particular, the power of $3$ in $\operatorname{Bi}(0)$ is
in the denominator.

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,$$

where for $t>0$ one uses the real logarithm convention
$t^{z-1}:=\exp((z-1)\log t)$.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the
displayed domain.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: By [F3], $\Gamma(2/3)>0$, so [F2] gives $\operatorname{Ai}(0)>0$; in particular, $\operatorname{Ai}$ is not the zero function. Put $u(t)=\operatorname{Ai}(-t)$. By [F1] and the chain rule in [F4], $u''(t)+tu(t)=0$ for real $t$.

Suppose $u$ has no zero on $[1,1+\pi]$. Continuity gives a constant sign; replace $u$ by $-u$ if necessary so that $u>0$ there. Set $W(t)=u'(t)\sin(t-1)-u(t)\cos(t-1)$. The product rule and sine and cosine derivatives in [F4], together with the equation in step 1.1, give $W'(t)=(1-t)u(t)\sin(t-1)\le0$ on this interval.
But $W(1)=-u(1)<0$ and $W(1+\pi)=u(1+\pi)>0$, contradicting that $W$ is nonincreasing. Therefore $u$ has a zero in $[1,1+\pi]$, and $\operatorname{Ai}$ has a zero in $[-(1+\pi),-1]$.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

If $\sum a_n=A$ and $\sum b_n=B$ converge absolutely in $\mathbb C$, and $c_n=\sum_{k\le n}a_kb_{n-k}$, then $\sum c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]], [[thm-complex-plane-is-complete]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[def-monoid-finite-product]], [[thm-generalised-associativity]], [[cor-cauchy-product-absolute]], [[thm-direct-comparison-test]], [[lem-series-linearity]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]].

Every absolutely convergent complex series converges, and every rearrangement has the same sum. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]], [[thm-absolute-convergence-in-rn]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

Let $a<b$ be reals. Suppose every $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is Riemann
integrable and $f_k\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$. Then $f$ is Riemann
integrable and

$$\int_a^b f_k\longrightarrow\int_a^b f.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

derivations.claim: For fixed $z$ and $|t|=1$, both exponential series in $$\exp\!\left(\frac z2(t-t^{-1})\right)= \left(\sum_{p\ge0}\frac{(z/2)^pt^p}{p!}\right) \left(\sum_{q\ge0}\frac{(-z/2)^qt^{-q}}{q!}\right)$$ have absolute tails bounded independently of $t$, by [F3]. Their product therefore has an absolutely and uniformly convergent double series on the unit circle; grouping its terms by the Laurent exponent $p-q$ is legitimate by [F4] and the absolute bound. For $n\ge0$, the coefficient of $t^n$ is $$\sum_{q\ge0}\frac{(-1)^q(z/2)^{2q+n}}{(q+n)!q!}=J_n(z)$$ by [F1]. Replacing the minus sign in the first exponential by a plus sign gives the coefficient $$\sum_{q\ge0}\frac{(z/2)^{2q+n}}{(q+n)!q!}=I_n(z).$$

For every integer $m$, direct integration of the real and imaginary parts gives $$\int_0^{2\pi}e^{im\theta}\,d\theta= \begin{cases}2\pi,&m=0,\\0,&m\ne0.\end{cases}$$ For $m\ne0$, the sine and cosine antiderivatives and their $2\pi$-periodicity from [F5] give zero. Integrating each finite Laurent partial sum against $e^{-in\theta}$ therefore extracts exactly its $t^n$ coefficient. The uniform convergence in step 1.1 permits passage to the full integral by [F6], applied componentwise. Consequently each coefficient is $$\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}G(e^{i\theta})e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta,$$ where $G$ is the corresponding generating function.

For real $x$, Euler's formula in [F5] gives $G_J(e^{i\theta})=\exp(ix\sin\theta)$ and $G_I(e^{i\theta})=\exp(x\cos\theta)$. In the first coefficient integral, the real part is $\cos(x\sin\theta-n\theta)$; the substitution $\theta\mapsto2\pi-\theta$ on $[\pi,2\pi]$, justified by [F7], shows that the imaginary parts cancel and the real parts on the two half intervals agree. Thus the coefficient is $\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\cos(n\theta-x\sin\theta)\,d\theta$. For the second integral, $\cos(2\pi-\theta)=\cos\theta$ and the sine Fourier terms cancel under the same substitution, giving $\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta$. This proves both representations.
For $x\ge0$, every term in the series for $I_n(x)$ is nonnegative, so $I_n(x)\ge0$. The integral gives $e^{-x}I_n(x)\le\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)}d\theta\le1$, since $1-\cos\theta\ge0$.

On $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\ell_+(z)=-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right).$$

Here $\operatorname{Log}$ is the principal logarithm from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], and
$\gamma_E$ denotes Euler's constant $\gamma$ from
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]. Both $z$ and $1+z/n$ lie in the
principal-logarithm domain. The local uniform convergence of this series
and the identity $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ are established by
[[lem-loggamma-series-convergence-and-gamma-identity]].

For every $z$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the series defining
$\ell_+(z)$ in [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]] converges locally
uniformly, defines a holomorphic function, and satisfies
$e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ for Euler's Gamma function on that half-plane.

The **Euler-Mascheroni constant** is

$$ \gamma:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1n-\log N\right), $$

provided the limit exists.

For $n\ge1$, let

$$H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k,\qquad \gamma_n=H_n-\log n.$$

The sequence $(\gamma_n)$ is strictly decreasing and is bounded below by
$1-\log2$. It therefore converges to a constant $\gamma$ satisfying
$0<\gamma<1$, and

$$H_n=\log n+\gamma+o(1).$$

Consequently, $H_n/\log n\to1$ as $n\to\infty$, with the quotient considered
for $n\ge2$.

$n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n$ as the positive integer $n$ tends to infinity.

Equivalently,

$$\frac{n!}{\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n}\longrightarrow1\qquad(n\to\infty,\ n\ge1).$$

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an

(the sign function); both witnesses are on the

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $E \subseteq [a,b]$ be finite
([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]), and let $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$
satisfy

$$g(x) \;=\; f(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b] \setminus E .$$

Then $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b g \;=\; \int_a^b f .$$

In particular the values of an integrand at the endpoints of the interval, and at
any finite set of points, are irrelevant to both questions.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Define $f(u)=\lfloor u\rfloor-u+1/2$. For $u=n+t$ with integer $n\ge0$ and $0\le t<1$, $f(u)=1/2-t$. Each full unit interval has integral zero, and its partial integral is $t(1-t)/2$. Therefore $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$, $\Phi(n)=0$, and $0\le\Phi\le1/8$.

On $[n,n+1]$, $\Phi'=f$ and [F7] gives $$\int_n^{n+1}\frac{f(u)}{u+z}\,du =\left[\frac{\Phi(u)}{u+z}\right]_{n}^{n+1} +\int_n^{n+1}\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du =\int_n^{n+1}\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du,$$ since $\Phi(n)=\Phi(n+1)=0$. Summing over $n<N$ gives $$I_N(z):=\int_0^N\frac{f(u)}{u+z}\,du =\int_0^N\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du.$$ Because $|u+z|\ge u+\operatorname{Re}z$ and $\Phi\le1/8$, the right-hand side converges absolutely as $N\to\infty$.

On each $[n,n+1]$, write $f(u)=n+\tfrac12-u=(n+z+\tfrac12)-(u+z)$. By [F5] the function $(n+z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(u+z)-u$ has derivative $f(u)/(u+z)$; its derivative is continuous and integrable on the compact interval by [F6]. Applying [F6] and summing the resulting endpoint differences yields $$I_N(z)=(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) -(z+\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z-N-\log((N-1)!) -zH_{N-1}+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\left(\frac zk-\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)\right).$$ The coefficient of each internal $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)$ in the endpoint sum is $-1$. For $k\ge1$, $\operatorname{Log}(k+z)=\log k+\operatorname{Log}(1+z/k)$ because $k>0$ is real and multiplication by it preserves the principal argument; [F9] gives $\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\log k=\log((N-1)!)$. These identities give the displayed form.

Add $-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez$ to the finite sum in step 2.2. By [F1]--[F3], the resulting left side converges to $\ell_+(z)$, while $$\ell_+(z)=I_N(z)-(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) +(z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z+N+\log((N-1)!) +z(H_{N-1}-\gamma_E)+o(1).$$

Taking logarithms in [F4] is valid by continuity [F8]. The laws [F9] and $e=\exp(1)$ give $$\log(n!)=(n+\tfrac12)\log n-n+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+o(1).$$ At $n=N-1$, since $\log(1-1/N)=-1/N+O(N^{-2})$, this becomes $$\log((N-1)!)=(N-\tfrac12)\log N-N+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)+o(1).$$ The logarithm estimate follows by integrating $1/(1-t)$ on $[0,1/N]$; the difference from $1/N$ is bounded by $1/(N^2(1-1/N))$. Also [F3] gives $H_{N-1}-\gamma_E=\log N+o(1)$. Finally, for fixed $z$ and $N>2|z|$, $$\operatorname{Log}(N+z)=\log N+z/N+O_z(N^{-2}),$$ since $N>0$ and $1+z/N,N+z$ lie in the right half-plane, so $\operatorname{Log}(N+z)=\log N+\operatorname{Log}(1+z/N)$. By [F5] and [F6], $\operatorname{Log}(1+w)-w=-\int_0^1tw^2/(1+tw)\,dt$ for $w=z/N$; here $|1+tw|\ge1$ when $\operatorname{Re}z>0$. Therefore $(N+z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(N+z) =(N+z-\tfrac12)\log N+z+o(1)$.

Substitute these asymptotics into step 3.1. The coefficients of $\log N$ cancel, and $N$ cancels the $-N$ in the factorial term, leaving $$\ell_+(z)=\lim_{N\to\infty}I_N(z) +(z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}z-z+\tfrac12\log(2\pi).$$ By step 2.1, the limit is the absolutely convergent integral of $\Phi(u)/(u+z)^2$. This is the claimed identity.

For real $x>0$, define
$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=e^{x^2}\operatorname{erfc}(x)$. For each integer
$k\ge0$, define the finite positive moment

$$M_k(x)=\int_0^\infty t^k e^{-t^2-2xt}\,dt.$$

The moments are auxiliary quantities for a finite-depth interval enclosure of
$\operatorname{erfcx}$. They are not the modified Bessel functions $I_k$.

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define the Fresnel functions and error function by

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

For the $k$th term $e_k$ of the $\operatorname{erf}$ series in
[[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]],

$$\frac{|e_{k+1}|}{|e_k|} =\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}\frac{2k+1}{2k+3} \le\frac{|z|^2}{k+1}.$$

Thus, if $|z|^2/(K+2)=q<1$, the tail after terms $0,\ldots,K$ is bounded by
$|e_{K+1}|/(1-q)$. The series converges locally uniformly and equals
$2/\sqrt\pi$ times the integral of $e^{-t^2}$ from $0$ to $z$.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\Gamma(z):=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt,$$

where for $t>0$ one uses the real logarithm convention
$t^{z-1}:=\exp((z-1)\log t)$.

The next lemma proves that the improper integral converges locally uniformly on
the open right half-plane, so this definition is well posed exactly on the
displayed domain.

The improper integral

$$\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt$$

converges locally uniformly on $\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

derivations.claim: The integrands in [F1] are positive. Near $0$ they are bounded by $t^k$. For $t\ge1$, $e^{-2xt}\le1$; the substitution $s=t^2$ and [F6] bound the tail by $\frac12\int_1^\infty s^{(k-1)/2}e^{-s}ds$, which is finite by the Gamma integral convergence in [F8]. The integrands are continuous on every compact truncation interval, so their proper integrals there exist by [F7]. Thus each $M_k$ is finite; it is strictly positive because its integrand is positive on $[1,2]$.

Apply [F5] on $[\varepsilon,R]$ to $w(t)=e^{-t^2-2xt}$ and to $t^kw(t)$. These functions and their derivatives are continuous on the compact interval, so all derivatives required by [F5] are integrable by [F7]; the complex-valued integration-by-parts statement is applied componentwise. The boundary terms tend to $0$ at $R\to\infty$; for $k\ge1$ they also tend to $0$ at $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, while for $k=0$ the lower boundary tends to $1$. For the infinite endpoint, choose an integer $m>k/2$; the exponential series gives $e^{t^2/2}\ge (t^2/2)^m/m!$, so $t^ke^{-t^2-2xt}\le 2^m m!t^{k-2m}e^{-t^2/2}\to0$. Passing to the limits in the integration-by-parts identities gives $2xM_0+2M_1=1$ and, for $k\ge1$, $kM_{k-1}=2xM_k+2M_{k+1}$.

Divide the recurrence with index $k+1$ by $2M_k>0$. Since $r_k=M_{k+1}/M_k$ and $r_{k+1}=M_{k+2}/M_{k+1}$, this gives $(k+1)/2=xr_k+r_kr_{k+1}$ and hence $r_k=(k+1)/(2(x+r_{k+1}))$. Positivity gives $0<r_k<(k+1)/(2x)$.

The integrand in [F4] is even, so $\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}du=\sqrt\pi/2$. Subtract the integral identity in [F3] and use the definition in [F2] to get $$\operatorname{erfc}(x)=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_x^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du.$$ The increasing substitution $u=t+x$ from [F6] then gives $$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-t^2-2xt}\,dt=\frac{2M_0}{\sqrt\pi}.$$ The first identity in step 2.1 gives $2M_0(x+r_0)=1$; substitution proves $\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=1/(\sqrt\pi(x+r_0))$.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

derivations.claim: The convergence of the first two formal derivative series in [F2], together with the infinite radius supplied by the ratio bound in [[lem-integer-order-bessel-series-tail]], lets [F3] justify each termwise differentiation used below. For a monomial $z^{2k+n}$, $(z^2D^2+zD-n^2)z^{2k+n}=4k(k+n)z^{2k+n}$. The coefficient ratio in [F1] is $a_k/a_{k-1}=\mp1/[4k(k+n)]$ for $k\ge1$, with the minus sign for $J_n$ and plus sign for $I_n$. Thus the coefficient of each power cancels in the respective differential equation.

For $J_{n-1}+J_{n+1}$, reindex the $J_{n+1}$ series so both terms have power $z^{2k+n-1}$. For $k\ge1$ their combined coefficient is $(-1)^kn/[2^{2k+n-1}k!(k+n)!]$, and for $k=0$ it is $1/[2^{n-1}(n-1)!]$. These are exactly the coefficients of $(2n/z)J_n$. For $I_{n-1}-I_{n+1}$ the same reindexing gives the same positive combined coefficient, proving the second recurrence.
Differentiating the $J_0$ series termwise by [F3] and reindexing $k=j+1$ gives $$J_0'(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{j+1}z^{2j+1}}{2^{2j+1}j!(j+1)!} =-J_1(z).$$
Setting $z=0$ in the convergent series leaves only the $k=0,n=0$ term; every term has a positive power of $z$ when $n\ge1$. Hence the stated limits hold.

On $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, define

$$\ell_+(z)=-\operatorname{Log}z-\gamma_Ez+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right).$$

Here $\operatorname{Log}$ is the principal logarithm from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]], and
$\gamma_E$ denotes Euler's constant $\gamma$ from
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]. Both $z$ and $1+z/n$ lie in the
principal-logarithm domain. The local uniform convergence of this series
and the identity $e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ are established by
[[lem-loggamma-series-convergence-and-gamma-identity]].

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

derivations.claim: Put $w=z/n$, so $\operatorname{Re}w>0$. The integrand in the path formula is continuous and integrable by [F4]. By [F2], [F3], and the chain rule, $$w-\operatorname{Log}(1+w)=\int_0^1\frac{tw^2}{1+tw}\,dt.$$ Since $|1+tw|^2=1+2t\operatorname{Re}w+t^2|w|^2\ge1$, this summand has modulus at most $|z|^2/(2n^2)$.

The decreasing function $t\mapsto t^{-2}$ satisfies $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}n^{-2}\le\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N$. Summing step 1.1 gives $|z|^2/(2N)$. Since $0<1-|z|/(N+1)<1$ under $N>2|z|$, this is no larger than the stated bound.

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

derivations.claim: For $\operatorname{Re}w>0$, the function $H(w)=\ell_+(w+1)-\ell_+(w)-\operatorname{Log}w$ is holomorphic by [F1], and $e^{H(w)}=1$ by [F1] and [F2]. Differentiating this identity by [F5] gives $e^{H(w)}H'(w)=0$, hence $H'(w)=0$ since $e^{H(w)}=1$. By [F6], $H$ is constant on the connected right half-plane. For positive real $w$, all three terms are real, so that constant is $0$. Therefore $\ell_+(w+1)=\ell_+(w)+\operatorname{Log}w$ throughout the right half-plane.

If $m_2>m_1$ are both admissible shifts, then $w=z+m_1$ has positive real part, as do $w,w+1,\ldots,w+(m_2-m_1-1)$. Iterating step 1.1 gives $$\ell_+(z+m_2)-\sum_{j=0}^{m_2-1}\operatorname{Log}(z+j) =\ell_+(z+m_1)-\sum_{j=0}^{m_1-1}\operatorname{Log}(z+j),$$ so the definition is independent of $m$. Locally $m$ can be fixed, making the formula holomorphic; independence makes these local formulas agree.

Exponentiating the formula with any admissible $m$ gives $e^{\ell(z)}=\Gamma(z+m)/\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(z+j)$ by [F1]. None of the factors vanishes because $z\in\Omega$. Iterating [F3] downward therefore identifies this quotient with $\Gamma(z)$.

Then $ds=2(t+x)dt$, $t+x=\sqrt{x^2+s}$, and $$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=\frac1{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-s}}{\sqrt{x^2+s}}\,ds =\frac1{x\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-s} \left(1+\frac{s}{x^2}\right)^{-1/2}ds.$$

Direct differentiation gives $f^{(N)}(u)=(-1)^N(1/2)_N(1+u)^{-N-1/2}$. Apply [F3] to $f(t)=(1+t)^{-1/2}$ at $0$ to obtain $$f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(-1)^k\frac{(1/2)_k}{k!}t^k+(-1)^N\rho_N(t), \qquad 0\le\rho_N(t)\le\frac{(1/2)_N}{N!}t^N \quad(t\ge0),$$ because $|f^{(N)}(u)|=(1/2)_N(1+u)^{-N-1/2}\le(1/2)_N$ for $u\ge0$.

Substitute $t=s/x^2$ in step 1.2 and integrate against $e^{-s}/(x\sqrt\pi)$. By the Gamma integral and [F4], $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}s^Nds=\Gamma(N+1)=N!$ by [F5] and [F4]. The signed remainder is nonnegative after removing $(-1)^N$ and is at most $(1/2)_N/(x^{2N+1}\sqrt\pi)$. The identity $(1/2)_N=(2N)!/(4^N N!)$ follows by separating even and odd factors in $(2N)!$. This gives the stated bound.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and

If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.

For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, let $\ell_+(z)$ be the branch in
[[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]]. Define
$$\Phi(u)=\int_0^u\bigl(\lfloor v\rfloor-v+1/2\bigr)\,dv.$$
Then the absolutely convergent integral satisfies
$$\ell_+(z)=\left(z-\frac12\right)\operatorname{Log}z-z+ \frac12\log(2\pi)+\int_0^\infty\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du.$$
On each unit interval, $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$ for $0\le t\le1$; hence
$0\le\Phi(u)\le1/8$.

derivations.claim: The formula in [F1] defines $\Phi(n+t)=t(1-t)/2$ for integer $n\ge0$ and $0\le t\le1$. Hence $0\le\Phi(u)\le1/8$ for every $u\ge0$.

Put $r=|z|$ and $\theta=\arg z$. Since $|\theta|<\pi/2\le\pi-\delta$, one has $\cos\theta\ge-\cos\delta$. Therefore $$|u+z|^2\ge u^2+r^2-2ur\cos\delta \ge\sin^2(\delta/2)(u+r)^2,$$ where the difference in the last inequality is $\cos^2(\delta/2)(u-r)^2\ge0$. Thus $|u+z|^{-2}\le\sin^{-2}(\delta/2)(u+r)^{-2}$.

Applying steps 1.1 and 1.2 to the remainder in [F1] gives $$|R(z)|\le\frac{1}{8\sin^2(\delta/2)}\int_0^\infty\frac{du}{(u+r)^2} =\frac{1}{8\sin^2(\delta/2)r}.$$ For any complex $w$, $|e^w-1|\le e^{|w|}-1$ by the exponential series; apply this with $w=R(z)$.

Fix $0<\delta\le\pi/2$ and $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.
For the branch $\ell_+$ from [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]],
[[lem-binet-loggamma-right-halfplane-identity]] gives
$$\ell_+(z)=\left(z-\frac12\right)\operatorname{Log}z-z+ \frac12\log(2\pi)+R(z), \qquad R(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du,$$
