For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of

with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final

accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive

check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining

evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all

its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

dyadic complex argument $z$, and, for the Gauss-series target, exact dyadic

tolerance $\varepsilon_a$, optional positive exact rational relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r$, a fixed exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$,
and finite positive integer caps $S_{\max},N_{\max},p_{\max},W$, with
$p_{\max}\ge2$. The stage
cap $S_{\max}$ bounds retries, $N_{\max}$ bounds series terms, $p_{\max}$
bounds dyadic precision, and $W$ bounds this procedure's exact interval
operations, term constructions, and elementary-DAG node operations. Every

stage $q$, use
precision $p=\max(2,\min(q,p_{\max}))$ and truncation index $q$ for every

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in

arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

For $z\ne0$, the functions in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]] satisfy

$$z^2J_n''+zJ_n'+(z^2-n^2)J_n=0, \qquad z^2I_n''+zI_n'-(z^2+n^2)I_n=0.$$

For real or complex $z\ne0$ and integer $n\ge1$, they also satisfy

$$J_{n-1}(z)+J_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}J_n(z), \qquad I_{n-1}(z)-I_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}I_n(z).$$

In addition, $J_0'(z)=-J_1(z)$.

At $z=0$, the series limits are $J_0(0)=I_0(0)=1$ and
$J_n(0)=I_n(0)=0$ for $n\ge1$.

Fix real $x>0$. Let $D_0(x)=-J_1(x)$ and $D_1(x)=J_0(x)$, and for every integer
$j\ge1$ define

$$D_{j+1}(x)=\frac{2j}{x}D_j(x)-D_{j-1}(x).$$

Thus $D$ is the second sequence obtained from the same order recurrence as
$J_j(x)$. It is a local auxiliary solution, not the Bessel function of the
second kind.
For every real $x>0$, $J_0(x)$ and $J_1(x)$ are not both zero.

derivations.claim: Using [F1] and [F2], for $j\ge1$, $$W_j=J_j\left(\frac{2j}{x}D_j-D_{j-1}\right) -\left(\frac{2j}{x}J_j-J_{j-1}\right)D_j =J_{j-1}D_j-J_jD_{j-1}=W_{j-1}.$$ Thus $W_j=W_0$ for every $j\ge0$.
By [F2], $W_0=J_0D_1-J_1D_0=J_0^2+J_1^2$, which is strictly positive by [F3]. A linear dependence of $J,D$ would make every $2\times2$ determinant $W_j$ zero, so they are independent.

derivations.claim: The sequence $J+qD$ obeys the recurrence by [F2] and [F3], and its value at $N+1$ is $J_{N+1}+qD_{N+1}=0$. Its value at $N$ is nonzero: if it too were zero, backward recurrence would make it zero at every index, contradicting the linear independence in [F1] and its coefficient $1$ on $J$. Therefore $(J+qD)/(J_N+qD_N)$ has the terminal values $u_{N+1}=0,u_N=1$. Uniqueness of the finite backward recurrence gives $u_j=(J_j+qD_j)/(J_N+qD_N)$ for $0\le j\le N$.

Taking the ratio of the formulas for $j=n$ and $j=s$ yields $u_n/u_s=(J_n+qD_n)/(J_s+qD_s)$. Since the denominator is nonzero, $$\widehat J_n-J_n =J_s\frac{J_n+qD_n}{J_s+qD_s}-J_n =\frac{q(J_sD_n-J_nD_s)}{J_s+qD_s}.$$ Every equality uses this single fixed terminal index $N$; no limit in $N$ was taken.

citations.quote:
Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Fix real $x>0$ and integer $N\ge0$. Set
$I_N=[0,(N+1)/(2x)]$, and for $k=N-1,\ldots,0$ define

$$I_k=\left[\frac{k+1}{2(x+\sup I_{k+1})}, \frac{k+1}{2(x+\inf I_{k+1})}\right].$$

Then $r_k\in I_k$ for every $0\le k\le N$, where $r_k$ is the moment ratio
from [[lem-erfcx-moment-recurrence]]. Therefore

$$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)\in \left[\frac1{\sqrt\pi(x+\sup I_0)}, \frac1{\sqrt\pi(x+\inf I_0)}\right].$$

Each finite depth gives a valid enclosure; no convergence or shrinking-width
claim as $N$ grows is made.

For real $x>0$ and integer $N\ge1$, put

$$(1/2)_0=1,\qquad (1/2)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(j+1/2).$$

$$S_N(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (-1)^k\frac{(1/2)_k}{x^{2k}}.$$

Then

$$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)-S_N(x)=(-1)^N R_N(x),\qquad 0\le R_N(x)\le \frac1{x\sqrt\pi}\frac{(2N)!}{4^N N!x^{2N}}.$$

This is a finite signed remainder bound, not a convergence assertion for the
asymptotic series.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

Input an exact dyadic real $x$, positive rational absolute tolerance
$\varepsilon_a$, optional positive rational relative tolerance
$\varepsilon_r$, a fixed exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, and finite
positive integer caps $S_{\max},D_{\max},N_{\max},p_{\max},W$, with
$p_{\max}\ge2$. Here
$S_{\max}$ bounds stages, $D_{\max}$ the continued-fraction depth,
$N_{\max}$ the asymptotic truncation, $p_{\max}$ the dyadic precision, and
$W$ the exact interval operations, terms, and subroutine calls performed by
this procedure. Reject nonpositive tolerances, invalid caps,
$e_{\min}>e_{\max}$, or $x\le0$ with domain. At stage $q$, use
$D=\min(q,D_{\max})$, $N=\min(q,N_{\max})$, precision
$p=\max(2,\min(q,p_{\max}))$, and truncation index $q$ for elementary-range calls.
Outputs and status meanings are those of
[[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]].

All rational and interval arithmetic uses
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. Charge every exact
arithmetic operation, range-evaluator node operation, term, rounding, and
loop update to the shared counter $W$. Interrupt any nested elementary-range
call with inconclusive before its next operation would exceed the remaining
budget. Return inconclusive before any local operation would exceed $W$. A
final endpoint overflow
returns range. A non-finite required arithmetic operation or elementary-range subcall makes its candidate unavailable; if neither candidate can be formed, the current stage is
inconclusive and later stages may still be tried.

For each stage $q=1,\ldots,S_{\max}$, compute $P_q$, a finite dyadic
interval containing $\pi$, as follows. For $r\in\{1/5,1/239\}$, form
$A_q(r)=\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}(-1)^jr^{2j+1}/(2j+1)$ and
$E_q(r)=r^{2q+1}/((2q+1)(1-r^2))$ exactly; the arctangent-tail lemma gives
$\arctan r\in[A_q(r)-E_q(r),A_q(r)+E_q(r)]$. Combine these intervals by
$\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$ and round outward to the selected
format at precision $p$. The Machin identity and tails are supplied by
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]. If the interval
conversion is non-finite, skip the stage. Call
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on the real one-node DAG
$\sqrt{P_q}$, using exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, precision $p$,
and truncation $q$. If this call is not finite or its output $R_q$ does
not have positive lower endpoint, skip this stage. Otherwise $R_q$ encloses
$\sqrt\pi$ by [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]].

Form the continued-fraction candidate as follows. Set
$I_D=[0,(D+1)/(2x)]$. For $k=D-1,\ldots,0$, set
$$I_k=\left[\frac{k+1}{2(x+\sup I_{k+1})}, \frac{k+1}{2(x+\inf I_{k+1})}\right]$$
by outward interval operations. Apply the decreasing map
$r\mapsto1/(\sqrt\pi(x+r))$ to $I_0$, evaluating $\sqrt\pi$ with
$R_q$, to obtain a candidate interval $C_q$. The finite-depth
containment lemma [[lem-erfcx-continued-fraction-enclosure]] makes $C_q$
a valid enclosure for every $D\ge0$.

If $N\ge1$, also form the asymptotic candidate. Evaluate
$$S_N(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(-1)^k\frac{(1/2)_k}{x^{2k}}, \qquad B_N(x)=\frac1{x\sqrt\pi}\frac{(2N)!}{4^NN!x^{2N}}$$
with $R_q$ and exact factorial/rational interval arithmetic. Write the computed sum interval as $[s_-,s_+]$ and take a nonnegative outward upper endpoint $b_N$ for the remainder bound $B_N$. Set
$A_q=[s_-,s_++b_N]$ when $N$ is even and
$A_q=[s_--b_N,s_+]$ when $N$ is odd, rounding the final endpoints outward. The signed remainder lemma
[[lem-erfcx-asymptotic-remainder]] makes $A_q$ a valid enclosure.

If both candidates are finite, intersect them when the intersection is
nonempty; if it is empty, discard the stage. If only one is finite, use that
candidate. Round the selected final endpoints outward to precision $p$.
Return success at the first stage whose radius is at most
$\varepsilon_a$. Set relative_certified to true exactly when relative
tolerance was requested, the interval excludes zero, and the contract's
relative-radius test passes; a failed relative test does not prevent absolute
success. If no stage passes before the finite caps, return inconclusive.

derivations.claim: A continued-fraction candidate contains $\operatorname{erfcx}(x)$ by [F1]. A signed-asymptotic candidate contains it by [F2]. The interval evaluation of each candidate is sound by [A1] and [A2]. If the procedure intersects both candidates, their common exact value lies in the intersection; otherwise the selected candidate remains an enclosure.
Thus every interval eligible for a success return contains the exact value. The finite arithmetic and intersection preserve inclusion by [A2] and the algorithm definition.

The procedure reports success only after the absolute-radius test in [F3] and sets a relative flag only when the interval excludes zero and the relative-radius test passes. No width decrease or universal success is asserted.

The stage loop is finite; every continued-fraction recurrence, asymptotic sum, and elementary-range call has finite depth, terms, format, and truncation index. Every branch has an explicit return or proceeds to the next bounded stage. Therefore every capped execution terminates.

citations.quote:
Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For any finite complex rectangle on which the principal branch is defined,
every finite output for a requested complex node of
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for $\exp$ or
$\operatorname{Log}$ contains the exact image. For the same typed DAG and
designated complex output node, nested input rectangles on the same admissible
branch, fixed constant enclosures, and the same finite dyadic format and
truncation index give nested finite enclosures whenever both calls return
finite results. Rectangles meeting zero, the negative real
branch cut, or an unresolved quadrant return the declared domain or
inconclusive status.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Inputs are a finite dyadic complex rectangle $Z$, a target label $\Gamma$ or
$\ell$, positive exact rational absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a$,
optional positive exact rational relative tolerance $\varepsilon_r$, a fixed
dyadic format precision $p_0\ge2$ and exponent range
$(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, fixed integer elementary truncation index $K\ge1$,
finite positive integer work cap $W$, and integer precision cap $P\ge p_0$.
The target
$\ell$ is the continued
branch in [[def-loggamma-slit-plane-branch]]. Reject an invalid target, empty or non-finite rectangle, invalid cap,
tolerance, $e_{\min}>e_{\max}$, or
$Z\not\subset\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ by returning
domain. The exact rectangle test is: either the imaginary interval omits
zero, or the real interval has strictly positive lower endpoint. Reject a
selected shift $m>W$ with inconclusive. For stages $q=1,\ldots,P$, use
precision $p=\max(p_0,q)$, harmonic cutoff $M=\min(q,W)$, product cutoff
$N=\min(q,W)$, and the fixed elementary truncation index $K$ for every
range call. Output statuses are those of
[[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]].

Use [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] for interval
arithmetic. Count every exact rational or interval operation, series term,
elementary-DAG node operation, rounding, and loop update against the shared
counter $W$. If the procedure is called by another evaluator, charge these
same primitive operations directly to that caller's shared counter, so the
caller can debit the actual child work; the local cap $W$ remains in force.
Before any operation would exceed either remaining cap, return inconclusive.
Run nested elementary-range calls under that counter and interrupt a subcall
before its next operation would exceed the remaining budget. A non-finite
range result makes the current candidate unavailable. Any other non-finite arithmetic result also makes its candidate unavailable; no partial result is retained. Final output overflow
returns range.

Choose
$$m=\max\!\left(0,\left\lfloor-\inf\Re Z\right\rfloor+1\right),$$
which is the least integer $m\ge0$ for which $\inf\Re Z+m>0$. Compute
this exactly from the rational endpoint; if $m>W$, return inconclusive
before forming the shift. Put $W_Z=Z+m$.
Before every elementary-range call, round each rational interval input
outward to the stage dyadic format; a conversion overflow makes that candidate
unavailable. A rounded Log input must still avoid the cut; otherwise its candidate is unavailable, rather than declaring the valid original input outside the domain. Embed a real interval $X$ explicitly as $X+i[0,0]$ whenever it participates in a complex expression; real and complex DAG nodes retain their declared types. All elementary-range calls below use
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the selected format and
fixed truncation $K$; its soundness for finite real and complex results is
given by
[[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]] and
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]].

For stage $q=1,\ldots,P$, form a dyadic $P_q$ containing $\pi$:
for $r\in\{1/5,1/239\}$, compute exactly
$A_q(r)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}(-1)^kr^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ and
$E_q(r)=r^{2q+1}/((2q+1)(1-r^2))$, combine
$\arctan r\in[A_q(r)-E_q(r),A_q(r)+E_q(r)]$ by the Machin identity, and
round outward to the selected format at precision $p$. These tails and the
identity are in
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]. If the conversion
is non-finite or $\inf P_q\le0$, the Stirling candidate is unavailable for
this stage; still attempt the product candidate. Let
$a_W=\inf\Re W_Z>0$ and
$R_W=\max(|\inf\Re W_Z|,|\sup\Re W_Z|)
+\max(|\inf\Im W_Z|,|\sup\Im W_Z|)$; $R_W$ is an exact rational upper
bound for $|w|$ on $W_Z$.

For this stage, call the elementary-range algorithm on the principal-log node
for each $Z+j$, $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Translation by these real integers
preserves avoidance of the cut for an input rectangle wholly in the slit
plane; if the exact branch-domain check fails, return domain. Add the finite
log rectangles to form the shift sum $L_Z$. If any shift-log call is non-finite, discard this whole stage, since both candidates require that sum. When $m=0$, set $L_Z=0$.

Construct the product candidate when $N>2R_W$. Call the elementary-range
algorithm for the real node $\log M$ to get an enclosure $G_M=[g_-,g_+]$ of
$\log M$, and form the outward-rounded Euler-constant interval
$[H_M-g_+-1/M,\ H_M-g_-]$, where $H_M=\sum_{k=1}^M1/k$ exactly. Call
the complex principal-log node on $W_Z$ and on each $1+W_Z/k$ for
$1\le k\le N$. All these rectangles lie in the principal-log domain since
$\Re W_Z>0$. Form
$$Q_N=-\operatorname{Log}(W_Z)-\gamma_E W_Z+ \sum_{k=1}^N\left(\frac{W_Z}{k}-\operatorname{Log}(1+W_Z/k)\right)$$
by interval arithmetic, and enlarge each coordinate by an outward upper bound for
$$T_N=\frac{R_W^2}{2N(1-R_W/(N+1))}.$$
The tail lemma [[lem-loggamma-product-tail-bound]] proves that this is an
enclosure of $\ell_+(W_Z)$, uniformly on the whole rectangle. Subtract
$L_Z$ to get the shifted product candidate for $\ell(Z)$. If $N\le2R_W$
or a required call is non-finite, this candidate is unavailable at this stage.

Construct the Stirling candidate only when $P_q$ is finite and has positive
lower endpoint. Call the complex principal-log node on $W_Z$, and the real
logarithm node on $2P_q$. Form
$$S_Z=(W_Z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(W_Z)-W_Z+ \tfrac12\log(2\pi)-L_Z$$
by interval arithmetic and enlarge each coordinate by an outward upper bound for $1/(4a_W)$.
The sectorial remainder lemma [[lem-sectorial-stirling-explicit-remainder-bound]]
proves this is an enclosure of $\ell(Z)$. If a required call is non-finite,
this candidate is unavailable at this stage.

If both log candidates are available, intersect them when the intersection is
nonempty; if empty, discard the stage. If only one is available, select it.
For target $\ell$, use this rectangle as the output candidate. For target
$\Gamma$, call the complex exponential node on the selected rectangle and
use its finite output rectangle. Return success at the first stage whose
candidate radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. Set relative_certified to true
exactly when relative tolerance was requested, zero is excluded, and the
contract's relative-radius test passes; a failed relative test does not
prevent absolute success. If no stage succeeds before its caps, return
inconclusive.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

For every $z\in\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, the value $\ell(z)$ in
[[def-loggamma-slit-plane-branch]] is independent of the integer $m\ge0$ with
$\operatorname{Re}(z+m)>0$, is holomorphic on $\Omega$, and satisfies
$e^{\ell(z)}=\Gamma(z)$.

For every $z$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, the series defining
$\ell_+(z)$ in [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]] converges locally
uniformly, defines a holomorphic function, and satisfies
$e^{\ell_+(z)}=\Gamma(z)$ for Euler's Gamma function on that half-plane.

For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$ and integer $N>2|z|$, the tail in the series for
$\ell_+(z)$ after its first $N$ summands satisfies

$$\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} \left(\frac zn-\operatorname{Log}\left(1+\frac zn\right)\right)\right| \le \frac{|z|^2}{2N\left(1-|z|/(N+1)\right)}.$$

For each integer $M\ge1$, put $H_M=\sum_{k=1}^M1/k$. Euler's constant
$\gamma$ satisfies
$$0\le H_M-\log M-\gamma\le\frac1M.$$
Thus $[H_M-\log M-1/M,\ H_M-\log M]$ is a finite enclosure for $\gamma$.

Fix $0<\delta\le\pi/2$ and $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}z>0$.
For the branch $\ell_+$ from [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]],
[[lem-binet-loggamma-right-halfplane-identity]] gives
$$\ell_+(z)=\left(z-\frac12\right)\operatorname{Log}z-z+ \frac12\log(2\pi)+R(z), \qquad R(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{\Phi(u)}{(u+z)^2}\,du,$$
where $\Phi(u)=\int_0^u(\lfloor v\rfloor-v+1/2)\,dv$. Then
$$|R(z)|\le \frac{1}{8\sin^2(\delta/2)|z|}.$$
For $\delta=\pi/2$, the bound is $1/(4|z|)$. The relative error after
exponentiating the three main terms is at most $\exp(|R(z)|)-1$.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

derivations.claim: For an admissible $Z$, the prescribed integer shift has $a_W=\inf\Re(Z+m)>0$. Translation by a nonnegative real integer preserves cut avoidance: either the imaginary interval omits zero, or the real lower endpoint was already positive. Thus each exact shift-log input lies in its domain. Its outward-rounded input still contains it; the procedure uses it only when its domain is certified. By [A1] the finite shift-log sum therefore encloses the corresponding exact sum for every $z\in Z$. An unavailable shift sum discards the stage and makes no finite claim.

Write $G_M=[g_-,g_+]$ for a finite enclosure of $\log M$. By [F5], the outward interval $[H_M-g_+-1/M,H_M-g_-]$ contains the same real $\gamma_E$ used by the branch. Finite outward evaluation of the product partial sum contains its exact value for every $w\in W_Z=Z+m$ by [A1]. The exact rational majorant $R_W$ bounds $|w|$ uniformly. When $N>2R_W$, [F4] bounds each omitted tail by $T_N=R_W^2/(2N(1-R_W/(N+1)))$, since the numerator increases and the positive denominator decreases when $|w|$ is replaced by $R_W$. The disk of radius $T_N$ lies in the coordinate rectangle used to enlarge the partial sum. Subtracting the containing shift-log sum from step 1.1 and using [F3] therefore encloses the full range $\ell(Z)$.

The finite Machin construction encloses $\pi$ by [F7]. Its positive interval and the real logarithm call enclose $\log(2\pi)$ by [A1]. Therefore the finite Stirling main-term rectangle contains the exact main term on $W_Z$. For every such $w$, $|w|\ge\Re w\ge a_W>0$, so [F6] gives $|R(w)|\le1/(4a_W)$. The prescribed outward coordinate enlargement contains this remainder disk. After subtracting the shift-log sum, [F3] again identifies every enclosed target as the same continued branch $\ell(z)$.

Either finite log candidate thus contains $\ell(Z)$; their coordinatewise intersection, when used, also contains that entire image. For a log-Gamma target the selected rectangle is therefore sound. For a Gamma target, [A1] encloses its complex exponential, and [F3] identifies the pointwise exponential with $\Gamma(z)$ for every $z\in Z$. This proves full input-range containment for both targets.

The algorithm tests the actual final outward rectangle's radius before reporting `success`, and sets a relative flag only when the rectangle excludes zero and passes the relative-radius test. By [F2] these arithmetic tests give exactly the stated absolute and reported relative guarantees. Failed or non-finite candidates are never used for a finite success claim; no finite-cap success guarantee is asserted.

The stage count is at most $P$, each shift and sum has a finite integer cutoff, and each elementary call has a finite DAG, format and truncation index. Moreover [F1] checks the shared counter before each local or nested primitive operation and loop update, interrupting before either its own or its caller's remaining work budget is exceeded. Consequently every capped invocation returns a status after finitely many charged operations, whether or not any candidate succeeds.
