citations.quote:
Inputs are a finite dyadic complex rectangle $Z$, a target label $\Gamma$ or
$\ell$, positive exact rational absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a$,
optional positive exact rational relative tolerance $\varepsilon_r$, a fixed
dyadic format precision $p_0\ge2$ and exponent range
$(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, fixed integer elementary truncation index $K\ge1$,
finite positive integer work cap $W$, and integer precision cap $P\ge p_0$.
The target
$\ell$ is the continued
branch in [[def-loggamma-slit-plane-branch]]. Reject an invalid target, empty or non-finite rectangle, invalid cap,
tolerance, $e_{\min}>e_{\max}$, or
$Z\not\subset\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ by returning
domain. The exact rectangle test is: either the imaginary interval omits
zero, or the real interval has strictly positive lower endpoint. Reject a
selected shift $m>W$ with inconclusive. For stages $q=1,\ldots,P$, use
precision $p=\max(p_0,q)$, harmonic cutoff $M=\min(q,W)$, product cutoff
$N=\min(q,W)$, and the fixed elementary truncation index $K$ for every
range call. Output statuses are those of
[[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]].

Use [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] for interval
arithmetic. Count every exact rational or interval operation, series term,
elementary-DAG node operation, rounding, and loop update against the shared
counter $W$. If the procedure is called by another evaluator, charge these
same primitive operations directly to that caller's shared counter, so the
caller can debit the actual child work; the local cap $W$ remains in force.
Before any operation would exceed either remaining cap, return inconclusive.
Run nested elementary-range calls under that counter and interrupt a subcall
before its next operation would exceed the remaining budget. A non-finite
range result makes the current candidate unavailable. Any other non-finite arithmetic result also makes its candidate unavailable; no partial result is retained. Final output overflow
returns range.

Choose
$$m=\max\!\left(0,\left\lfloor-\inf\Re Z\right\rfloor+1\right),$$
which is the least integer $m\ge0$ for which $\inf\Re Z+m>0$. Compute
this exactly from the rational endpoint; if $m>W$, return inconclusive
before forming the shift. Put $W_Z=Z+m$.
Before every elementary-range call, round each rational interval input
outward to the stage dyadic format; a conversion overflow makes that candidate
unavailable. A rounded Log input must still avoid the cut; otherwise its candidate is unavailable, rather than declaring the valid original input outside the domain. Embed a real interval $X$ explicitly as $X+i[0,0]$ whenever it participates in a complex expression; real and complex DAG nodes retain their declared types. All elementary-range calls below use
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] with the selected format and
fixed truncation $K$; its soundness for finite real and complex results is
given by
[[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]] and
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]].

For stage $q=1,\ldots,P$, form a dyadic $P_q$ containing $\pi$:
for $r\in\{1/5,1/239\}$, compute exactly
$A_q(r)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}(-1)^kr^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ and
$E_q(r)=r^{2q+1}/((2q+1)(1-r^2))$, combine
$\arctan r\in[A_q(r)-E_q(r),A_q(r)+E_q(r)]$ by the Machin identity, and
round outward to the selected format at precision $p$. These tails and the
identity are in
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]. If the conversion
is non-finite or $\inf P_q\le0$, the Stirling candidate is unavailable for
this stage; still attempt the product candidate. Let
$a_W=\inf\Re W_Z>0$ and
$R_W=\max(|\inf\Re W_Z|,|\sup\Re W_Z|)
+\max(|\inf\Im W_Z|,|\sup\Im W_Z|)$; $R_W$ is an exact rational upper
bound for $|w|$ on $W_Z$.

For this stage, call the elementary-range algorithm on the principal-log node
for each $Z+j$, $j=0,\ldots,m-1$. Translation by these real integers
preserves avoidance of the cut for an input rectangle wholly in the slit
plane; if the exact branch-domain check fails, return domain. Add the finite
log rectangles to form the shift sum $L_Z$. If any shift-log call is non-finite, discard this whole stage, since both candidates require that sum. When $m=0$, set $L_Z=0$.

Construct the product candidate when $N>2R_W$. Call the elementary-range
algorithm for the real node $\log M$ to get an enclosure $G_M=[g_-,g_+]$ of
$\log M$, and form the outward-rounded Euler-constant interval
$[H_M-g_+-1/M,\ H_M-g_-]$, where $H_M=\sum_{k=1}^M1/k$ exactly. Call
the complex principal-log node on $W_Z$ and on each $1+W_Z/k$ for
$1\le k\le N$. All these rectangles lie in the principal-log domain since
$\Re W_Z>0$. Form
$$Q_N=-\operatorname{Log}(W_Z)-\gamma_E W_Z+ \sum_{k=1}^N\left(\frac{W_Z}{k}-\operatorname{Log}(1+W_Z/k)\right)$$
by interval arithmetic, and enlarge each coordinate by an outward upper bound for
$$T_N=\frac{R_W^2}{2N(1-R_W/(N+1))}.$$
The tail lemma [[lem-loggamma-product-tail-bound]] proves that this is an
enclosure of $\ell_+(W_Z)$, uniformly on the whole rectangle. Subtract
$L_Z$ to get the shifted product candidate for $\ell(Z)$. If $N\le2R_W$
or a required call is non-finite, this candidate is unavailable at this stage.

Construct the Stirling candidate only when $P_q$ is finite and has positive
lower endpoint. Call the complex principal-log node on $W_Z$, and the real
logarithm node on $2P_q$. Form
$$S_Z=(W_Z-\tfrac12)\operatorname{Log}(W_Z)-W_Z+ \tfrac12\log(2\pi)-L_Z$$
by interval arithmetic and enlarge each coordinate by an outward upper bound for $1/(4a_W)$.
The sectorial remainder lemma [[lem-sectorial-stirling-explicit-remainder-bound]]
proves this is an enclosure of $\ell(Z)$. If a required call is non-finite,
this candidate is unavailable at this stage.

If both log candidates are available, intersect them when the intersection is
nonempty; if empty, discard the stage. If only one is available, select it.
For target $\ell$, use this rectangle as the output candidate. For target
$\Gamma$, call the complex exponential node on the selected rectangle and
use its finite output rectangle. Return success at the first stage whose
candidate radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. Set relative_certified to true
exactly when relative tolerance was requested, zero is excluded, and the
contract's relative-radius test passes; a failed relative test does not
prevent absolute success. If no stage succeeds before its caps, return
inconclusive.

For any finite dyadic rectangle $Z\subset\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$,
whenever [[alg-certified-gamma-loggamma-evaluation]] returns `success`, its
returned enclosure contains the range of $\Gamma$ or the continued log-Gamma
branch on $Z$ and passes the stated absolute-radius test. Any reported
relative certificate obeys the zero-exclusion condition. No assertion
guarantees success for every valid input or finite cap. Every execution with
finite caps terminates.

Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

The coefficient recurrence in [[def-airy-initial-value-series]] makes both
series solve $y''=zy$. In a residue class $k\equiv r\pmod 3$, successive
nonzero terms have absolute ratio

$$\frac{|z|^3}{(k+3)(k+2)}.$$

If the ratio of each term after a chosen first omitted term is bounded by
$q<1$, that class's tail is at most the first omitted term's absolute value
divided by $1-q$. The series and their first two derivative series converge
locally uniformly on $\mathbb C$.

Inputs are an exact dyadic complex number $z$, a target label
$\operatorname{Ai}$ or $\operatorname{Bi}$, positive rational absolute
tolerance $\varepsilon_a$, optional positive rational relative tolerance
$\varepsilon_r$, a fixed exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, and finite
positive integer caps $S_{\max},K_{\max},p_{\max},W$, with $p_{\max}\ge2$.
Reject an invalid target, nonpositive tolerance, invalid cap, or
$e_{\min}>e_{\max}$ with domain. The caps bound stages,
terms per residue class, final dyadic precision, and this procedure's exact
interval operations and subroutine calls. For stage $q$, use $K=q$,
precision $p=\max(2,\min(q,p_{\max}))$, and elementary-range truncation $q$;
run stages $q=1,\ldots,\min(S_{\max},K_{\max},p_{\max})$.

All arithmetic uses [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]].
Charge every exact arithmetic operation, range-evaluator node operation,
term, rounding, and loop update to the shared counter $W$. Return
inconclusive before any local operation would exceed $W$; interrupt a nested
subroutine before its next operation would exceed the remaining budget. When
nested, charge every Gamma-child operation directly to the same parent counter.
If a final
endpoint overflows, return range. A non-finite subroutine result makes the
current stage unavailable; later stages may still be tried. Other statuses
are those of [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]].

At stage $q$, outward-round the rational points $1/3$ and $2/3$ to
dyadic intervals $G_r$ at precision $p$. For each $r\in\{1/3,2/3\}$, charge the
child-call operation to the parent counter. If no parent work unit remains,
return inconclusive; otherwise pass the positive remaining budget as the
child's work cap and call
[[alg-certified-gamma-loggamma-evaluation]] with target $\Gamma$ on the
complex rectangle $G_r+i[0,0]$, absolute tolerance $2^{-q}$, no relative
tolerance, the same exponent range, fixed elementary truncation $q$,
base format precision $p$, and precision cap $p$. Debit every operation
performed by the Gamma child to the shared counter. A
success output rectangle encloses
$\Gamma(r)$, since $r\in G_r$; if either call is not successful or its
rectangle contains zero, skip this stage. A failed rational-to-dyadic conversion also makes the stage unavailable.

For $s\in\{1/6,1/3,2/3\}$, outward-round the exact rational $s$ to a
dyadic interval $S_{s,p}$, then call
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on the real expression DAG
$\exp(S_{s,p}\log 3)$, with the same exponent range, precision $p$, and
truncation $q$. These calls enclose $3^s$ by
[[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]]. If a required call is not finite,
skip this stage. Embed each real power interval $X$ as the complex rectangle $X+i[0,0]$, then combine it with the Gamma rectangles by outward complex arithmetic
to enclose the two initial coefficients
$$(a_0,a_1)=\left(\frac{1}{3^{2/3}\Gamma(2/3)}, -\frac{1}{3^{1/3}\Gamma(1/3)}\right)$$
for Ai, or
$$(b_0,b_1)=\left(\frac{1}{3^{1/6}\Gamma(2/3)}, \frac{3^{1/6}}{\Gamma(1/3)}\right)$$
for Bi. If any divisor rectangle contains zero or an arithmetic operation is non-finite, skip this stage.

Put $R=|\Re z|+|\Im z|$, an exact rational upper bound for $|z|$.
For each residue $r=0,1$, initialize $t_{r,0}=c_r z^r$ using the
selected pair of initial coefficient intervals, and compute
$t_{r,j+1}=t_{r,j}z^3/((k+3)(k+2))$, where $k=r+3j$. Sum
$t_{r,0},\ldots,t_{r,q-1}$ and compute the first omitted term
$t_{r,q}$. Put $k_r=r+3q$ and
$$\rho_r=\frac{R^3}{(k_r+3)(k_r+2)}.$$
If either $\rho_r\ge1$, skip the stage. Otherwise enlarge the sum of both
partial rectangles in each coordinate by
$$\frac{M(t_{0,q})}{1-\rho_0}+\frac{M(t_{1,q})}{1-\rho_1},$$
where $M(X+iY)=\max(|\inf X|,|\sup X|)
+\max(|\inf Y|,|\sup Y|)$. The $c_2=0$ residue class vanishes identically.
The ratio and tail lemma [[lem-airy-series-coefficient-recurrence-and-tail]]
therefore makes the enlarged rectangle a containing enclosure of the selected
Airy value.

Round the final rectangle outward to precision $p$. Return success at the
first stage whose radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. Set relative_certified
to true exactly when relative tolerance was requested, zero is excluded, and
the contract's relative-radius test passes; a failed relative test does not
prevent absolute success. If no stage succeeds before its caps, return
inconclusive. The stage loop and all subroutine calls have finite caps, so the
procedure has no unbounded retry.

derivations.claim: The initial coefficients used by the procedure enclose the exact Airy initial values by [F3], with the Gamma calls sound by [A1] and the powers of 3 sound by [A2]. Arithmetic on these intervals is sound by [A3]. The series definition and recurrence determine all later coefficients, so the resulting partial sums enclose their exact finite series sums.

By [F2], each nonzero omitted class tail lies within its computed absolute tail bound; the third class is zero because its initial coefficient is zero and the recurrence preserves zero. Therefore the exact Airy value lies in the partial-sum enclosure enlarged by the sum of the two tail bounds.

The algorithm reports success only when that containing rectangle passes the requested radius test, and its relative flag obeys [F1]. If its finite caps do not allow that test, the result is inconclusive; no claim of universal success is made.

The stage loop is finite; each Gamma and elementary-range subcall has finite caps and truncation index, and the residue-class sums have at most the capped number of terms. Thus every capped execution terminates.

citations.quote:
Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Inputs are an integer order $n\ge0$, a target $J$ or scaled $I$, an exact
dyadic real argument $x$, positive rational absolute tolerance
$\varepsilon_a$, optional positive rational relative tolerance
$\varepsilon_r$, a fixed exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$, and finite
positive integer caps $S_{\max},K_{\max},M_{\max},N_{\max},p_{\max},W$, with
$p_{\max}\ge2$.
The caps bound stages, series terms, midpoint panels, Miller terminal index,
dyadic precision, and exact interval operations and subroutine calls. Run
stages $q=1,\ldots,\min(S_{\max},K_{\max},M_{\max},p_{\max})$, using precision
$p=\max(2,\min(q,p_{\max}))$ and elementary-range truncation $q$. Reject
$n<0$, invalid targets, nonpositive tolerances, invalid caps,
$e_{\min}>e_{\max}$, or $x<0$ for the scaled $I$ target with
domain. The scaled
target is always $e^{-x}I_n(x)$.

Use exact rational endpoint formulas for finite sums, recurrences, mesh
construction, and error bounds, with final endpoints rounded outward to
precision $p$. Charge every exact arithmetic operation, range-evaluator
node operation, term, rounding, and loop update to the shared counter $W$;
interrupt a nested elementary-range call with inconclusive before its next
operation would exceed the remaining budget. Factorials use
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. Call
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] for the real sine, cosine, and
exponential ranges in the midpoint branches. Before each call, round its
rational input interval outward to the fixed dyadic format. Its finite outputs are sound by
[[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]]. Count each exact operation, term,
rounding, and subroutine call against $W$; if the next operation would
exceed $W$, return inconclusive. A non-finite elementary call makes that
branch unavailable. Final endpoint overflow returns range.

Before forming any stage constant, if the target is scaled $I$ and $x=0$,
use precision $p=p_{\max}$, form $[1,1]$ when $n=0$ and $[0,0]$ when $n\ge1$, and round its
endpoints outward to that format. If either conversion overflows,
return range. Otherwise apply the ordinary absolute-radius test to the rounded candidate and return `success` only when it passes; return `inconclusive` if it fails. The internal exact candidate has radius zero, but outward underflow may widen its stored enclosure. Set a successful output's relative flag by the usual contract test, so a zero value
receives no relative certificate. This branch does not call the
elementary-range procedure.

At stage $q$, compute an outward dyadic interval $P_q$ containing $\pi$
from the Machin identity and alternating arctangent tails in
[[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]: for
$r=1/5,1/239$, use the $q$-term sum
$\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}(-1)^kr^{2k+1}/(2k+1)$ and tail bound
$r^{2q+1}/((2q+1)(1-r^2))$, combine by $16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$,
and round outward to the selected format at precision $p$. If this
conversion is non-finite or $\inf P_q\le0$, midpoint candidates are
unavailable at this stage; the independent power-series or Miller branches may
still be attempted.

For a requested $J_n(x)$, first form a power-series candidate if possible.
For any order $r\ge0$, define the finite subroutine $\operatorname{SeriesJ}(r)$:
start
$a_0=(x/2)^r/(0!\,r!)$ and
$a_{k+1}=-a_kx^2/(4(k+1)(k+r+1))$; sum $a_0,\ldots,a_{q-1}$, and
compute $a_q$. Put
$$\rho_J=\frac{x^2}{4(q+1)(q+r+1)}.$$
If $\rho_J<1$, return the interval partial sum enlarged by
$|a_q|/(1-\rho_J)$; otherwise mark this series candidate unavailable.
The tail lemma [[lem-integer-order-bessel-series-tail]] proves each returned
interval contains $J_r(x)$.

For each requested target, also form its composite-midpoint candidate with
$m=q$ panels, $h=\pi/m$, and nodes $\theta_j=(j+\tfrac12)h$,
$j=0,\ldots,m-1$, using $P_q$ as the interval for $\pi$. For $J_n$,
call the elementary-range algorithm for $\sin(\theta_j)$, form
$n\theta_j-x\sin(\theta_j)$, and call it for the cosine of that interval.
Let $Q_m$ be the interval sum $h\sum_j\cos(n\theta_j-x\sin\theta_j)$ and
$$E_J=\frac{h_{\max}^2}{24}\bigl((n+|x|)^2+|x|\bigr), \qquad h_{\max}=\sup(P_q)/m.$$
The candidate is $Q_m/P_q+[-E_J,E_J]$.
For the scaled $I$ target with $x>0$, call the elementary algorithm for
$\cos(\theta_j)$, form
$-x(1-\cos(\theta_j))$, call it for the real exponential, and also call it
for $\cos(n\theta_j)$. Let $Q_m$ be $h$ times the sum of the resulting
product intervals and set
$$E_I=\frac{h_{\max}^2}{24}\bigl((x+n)^2+x\bigr).$$
The candidate is $Q_m/P_q+[-E_I,E_I]$. The exact midpoint error lemmas
[[lem-bessel-integral-midpoint-error]] and
[[lem-scaled-modified-bessel-midpoint-error]] prove these inclusions.

For a $J_n(x)$ Miller candidate, only try this branch when $x>0$ and
$N=n+q\le N_{\max}$. Obtain $\operatorname{SeriesJ}(r)$ for
$r=0,1,n,N+1$; if any is unavailable, skip the branch. Set
$D_0=-J_1$, $D_1=J_0$, and compute
$D_{j+1}=2jD_j/x-D_{j-1}$ for $j=1,\ldots,N$ by interval arithmetic.
Set $u_{N+1}=0,u_N=1$, and compute
$u_{j-1}=2ju_j/x-u_{j+1}$ for $j=N,\ldots,1$. Require the intervals for
$D_{N+1}$, $u_s$, $J_s$, and $J_s+q_MD_s$ below to exclude zero. Form
$q_M=-J_{N+1}/D_{N+1}$. In the fixed order $s=0,1$, whenever the tests
pass, form
$$\widehat J_n=\frac{J_su_n}{u_s},\qquad E_M=\frac{q_M(J_sD_n-J_nD_s)}{J_s+q_MD_s}, \qquad C_M=\widehat J_n-E_M.$$
The exact finite terminal-contamination identity
[[lem-finite-miller-terminal-error-identity]] proves that each $C_M$
contains $J_n(x)$. The Casoratian lemma
[[lem-bessel-casoratian-invariant-positive]] supplies the independent
recurrence pair and positive invariant required by that identity.

Collect every available sound candidate for the requested target. If more
than one is available, intersect them; if the intersection is empty, discard
this stage. Round the selected candidate outward to precision $p$. Return
success at the first stage whose radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. Set
relative_certified to true exactly when relative tolerance was requested,
zero is excluded, and the contract's relative-radius test passes; failure of
that relative test does not prevent absolute success. If no stage succeeds
before the finite caps, return inconclusive. No branch uses a limit in the
Miller terminal index.

For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

Every integral below is the oriented Riemann integral constructed from upper
and lower Darboux sums in
[[lem-continuous-functions-riemann-integrable]]. It exists for each displayed
continuous integrand on the finite interval between its endpoints, is additive
in intervals, reverses sign when the endpoints are reversed, is monotone in
the integrand, and satisfies
$|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt|\le|b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|$.
These properties also
give constant comparison bounds and the average-value difference quotient
used to differentiate the integral-defined functions.

The exponential is $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!$ for $x\in\mathbb R$.
The sine and cosine are the everywhere-convergent power series
$\sin x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\cos x=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k x^{2k}/(2k)!$. Define
$\arctan x=\int_0^x dt/(1+t^2)$ and set $\pi=4\arctan1$. The natural
logarithm $\ln$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ by $\ln x=\int_1^x dt/t$.

The square root is the unique nonnegative real $y$ with $y^2=x$ for $x\ge0$;
existence and uniqueness follow from
[[lem-nonnegative-square-root-exists-and-unique]]. The tangent is
$\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on the set where $\cos x\ne0$.

For complex $z=x+iy$, the modulus $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is defined in
[[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. The complex exponential is
$\exp(x+iy)=\exp(x)(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The principal complex logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(z)=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}(z)$ on
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z=x+iy$ in this domain, define
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\ \pi/2,&x=0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi/2,&x=0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
The excluded negative real axis is the remaining case $x<0,y=0$; zero is
also excluded.

These are point functions. An interval extension must separately enclose their
exact ranges, test the stated domains, and return a non-finite status when its
finite budget cannot certify a reduction or endpoint.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

Fix $x>0$, integers $N\ge1$ and $0\le n<N$, and define the exact backward
recurrence solution by $u_{N+1}=0$, $u_N=1$, and
$u_{j-1}=2ju_j/x-u_{j+1}$ for $j=N,N-1,\ldots,1$. If
$D_{N+1}(x)\ne0$, put $q=-J_{N+1}(x)/D_{N+1}(x)$. For $s\in\{0,1\}$ such
that $J_s(x)+qD_s(x)\ne0$, let
$\widehat J_n=J_s(x)u_n/u_s$. Then

$$\widehat J_n-J_n= \frac{q\bigl(J_sD_n-J_nD_s\bigr)}{J_s+qD_s}.$$

This is a finite-$N$ identity. It makes no assertion that the error tends to
zero as $N\to\infty$.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, $x\in\mathbb R$, $m\ge1$, and $h=\pi/m$. Put
$\phi(\theta)=\cos(n\theta-x\sin\theta)$ and
$Q_m=h\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\phi((j+1/2)h)$. Then

$$\left|J_n(x)-\frac{Q_m}{\pi}\right| \le \frac{h^2}{24}\left((n+|x|)^2+|x|\right).$$

This is the local composite-midpoint certificate for the Bessel integral; it
does not certify floating-point summation unless each operation is enclosed.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, $x\ge0$, $m\ge1$, $h=\pi/m$, and
$$f(\theta)=e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)}\cos(n\theta),\qquad Q_m=h\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}f((j+1/2)h).$$
Then
$$\left|e^{-x}I_n(x)-\frac{Q_m}{\pi}\right| \le \frac{h^2}{24}\bigl((x+n)^2+x\bigr).$$
The bound certifies the exact midpoint integral. Floating-point summation is
certified only if its operations are enclosed separately.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

derivations.claim:
If the target is scaled $I$ and $x=0$, the defining series [F2] gives
$e^{-x}I_n(x)=1$ for $n=0$ and $0$ for $n\ge1$, so the exact internal singleton contains the target; its final outward conversion also contains it by [A2], and the algorithm tests the actual rounded radius. Otherwise, the power-series candidate contains
$J_n(x)$ by [F4]. The two midpoint candidates contain their integrals by [F6]
and [F7]; their finite sine, cosine, and exponential ranges are sound by
[A1], their mesh constant is enclosed by [F8], and their arithmetic interval
operations are sound by [A2]. The Miller candidate contains $J_n(x)$ because
its interval evaluates the exact error expression in [F5] and subtracts that
interval from the normalized backward value, using sound interval operations
[A2].
Every candidate used by the procedure therefore contains the same exact requested value. Any nonempty intersection of candidates also contains that value.

The algorithm reports success only after the containing interval passes the absolute-radius test and, when reported, the zero-excluding relative test in [F3]. Otherwise it returns an inconclusive or range status under finite caps. Thus the success claims are sound and do not rely on a limit as the Miller terminal index grows.

The stage and candidate loops are finite, every series and recurrence uses at most its stated finite index, and each elementary-range call has a finite DAG, format, and truncation index. Hence every capped execution terminates.

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define the Fresnel functions and error function by

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.

Let $S=\mathbb C\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}$ be the slit plane. Then $S$ is
a complex domain, star-shaped with respect to $1$, and homologically simply
connected. The principal logarithm $\operatorname{Log}$
([[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]]) is the
unique holomorphic $F:S\to\mathbb C$ with

$$\exp(F(z))=z\ \ (z\in S)\qquad\text{and}\qquad F(1)=0,$$

and it satisfies $\operatorname{Log}'(z)=1/z$ on $S$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $f(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ have radius $R$, and define

$$G(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{\iota(n+1)}(x-c)^{n+1}.$$

For every closed interval $[u,v]$ strictly inside $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is Riemann integrable and

$$\int_u^v f(x)\,dx=G(v)-G(u)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{\iota(n+1)}\bigl((v-c)^{n+1}-(u-c)^{n+1}\bigr).$$

Thus the power series may be integrated term by term, and the antiderivative series has radius $R$.

Inputs are a target label $T\in\{C,S,\operatorname{erf},{}_2F_1\}$, an exact
dyadic complex argument $z$, and, for the Gauss-series target, exact dyadic
complex parameters $a,b,c$. Also input positive exact rational absolute
tolerance $\varepsilon_a$, optional positive exact rational relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r$, a fixed exponent range $(e_{\min},e_{\max})$,
and finite positive integer caps $S_{\max},N_{\max},p_{\max},W$, with
$p_{\max}\ge2$. The stage
cap $S_{\max}$ bounds retries, $N_{\max}$ bounds series terms, $p_{\max}$
bounds dyadic precision, and $W$ bounds this procedure's exact interval
operations, term constructions, and elementary-DAG node operations. Every
nested elementary-range call shares this counter and is interrupted with
inconclusive before its next operation would exceed the remaining budget. At
stage $q$, use
precision $p=\max(2,\min(q,p_{\max}))$ and truncation index $q$ for every
elementary-range subcall.

Reject an invalid target, nonpositive tolerance, invalid cap, invalid exponent
range $e_{\min}>e_{\max}$, or a Gauss input with
$|z|^2\ge1$ or $c\in\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ by returning domain. The
Fresnel and error-function branches accept every finite complex $z$.
Outputs are a finite interval or rectangle with status success, or a
status inconclusive, domain, or range as in
[[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]].

[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. Embed real coefficient intervals $X$ as $X+i[0,0]$ in complex arithmetic; typed elementary DAG nodes never use an implicit real-to-complex conversion. If a required
intermediate operation or output endpoint overflows its selected format,
return range. If an elementary-range subcall returns a non-finite status,
skip the current candidate; if no later stage succeeds, return inconclusive.
Charge each exact arithmetic operation, coefficient term, rounding, and
elementary-range call against $W$; before an operation that would exceed
$W$, return inconclusive.

At each stage, form $P_q$, a certified dyadic interval containing $\pi$,
only when $T\in\{C,S,\operatorname{erf}\}$. For $r\in\{1/5,1/239\}$, form
$A_q(r)=\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}(-1)^jr^{2j+1}/(2j+1)$ and
$E_q(r)=r^{2q+1}/((2q+1)(1-r^2))$ by exact rational arithmetic. The
arctangent tail in [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
gives $\arctan r\in[A_q(r)-E_q(r),A_q(r)+E_q(r)]$. Combine these intervals
as $16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$, then round the resulting endpoints
outward to the selected format at precision $p$. The Machin identity in
that same lemma proves $\pi\in P_q$. If this conversion is non-finite,
skip this stage for the selected Fresnel or erf target. For the Gauss-series
target, omit $P_q$ and all square-root calls.

Only when $T=\operatorname{erf}$, call
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on the one-node real DAG
$\sqrt{P_q}$ with the same exponent range and precision $p$, and truncation
index $q$. If it returns a finite interval $R_q$, continue only if
$\inf R_q>0$; otherwise skip this stage. This call encloses $\sqrt\pi$
by [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]]. The $C,S$ branches use $P_q$
directly and do not call square root. For a complex rectangle
$B=X+iY$, write
$M(B)=\max(|\inf X|,|\sup X|)+\max(|\inf Y|,|\sup Y|)$; this rational
quantity bounds the modulus of every point in $B$.

At each stage $q=1,\ldots,\min(S_{\max},N_{\max},p_{\max})$, form the
following candidate for the selected target.

- For $C$, sum its defining terms $c_0,\ldots,c_{q-1}$ from
  [[def-fresnel-erf-and-hypergeometric-series]] by interval arithmetic,
  using $P_q/2$ for $\pi/2$. Let $c_q$ be the first omitted term and set
  $$r_C=\frac{(\sup P_q)^2 M(z)^4}{4(2q+1)(2q+2)}.$$
  If $r_C<1$, enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both coordinates by
  $M(c_q)/(1-r_C)$; otherwise skip this stage.
- For $S$, sum its first $q$ defining terms using $P_q/2$, let $s_q$
  be the first omitted term, and set
  $$r_S=\frac{(\sup P_q)^2 M(z)^4}{4(2q+2)(2q+3)}.$$
  If $r_S<1$, enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both coordinates by
  $M(s_q)/(1-r_S)$; otherwise skip this stage.
- For erf, use the interval $2/R_q$ from the single square-root call above
  for $2/\sqrt\pi$,
  sum the first $q$ defining terms, and let $e_q$ be the first omitted
  term. Set $r_E=M(z)^2/(q+1)$. If $r_E<1$, enlarge the partial-sum
  rectangle in both coordinates by $M(e_q)/(1-r_E)$; otherwise skip this
  stage.
- For the Gauss series, compute its terms by $h_0=1$ and
  $$h_{k+1}=h_k\,z\,\frac{(a+k)(b+k)}{(c+k)(k+1)}$$
  using exact interval operations. No denominator $c+k$ vanishes by the
  domain check. If $a$ or $b$ is a nonpositive integer, let $L$ be one
  more than the smaller absolute value of those nonpositive integer
  parameters. If $L\le q$, sum exactly through $h_{L-1}$ and use zero
  tail. Otherwise put
  $$A=|\Re a|+|\Im a|,\quad B=|\Re b|+|\Im b|,\quad C_0=|\Re c|+|\Im c|,\quad Z_0=|\Re z|+|\Im z|,$$
  and
  $$r_H=Z_0\frac{(1+A/q)(1+B/q)}{1-C_0/q}.$$
  If $q>C_0$ and $r_H<1$, sum $h_0,\ldots,h_{q-1}$, let $h_q$
  be the first omitted term, and enlarge the partial-sum rectangle in both
  coordinates by $M(h_q)/(1-r_H)$; otherwise skip this stage. The geometric
  bound in [[lem-gauss-hypergeometric-series-geometric-tail]] applies because
  $A,B,C_0,Z_0$ dominate the corresponding complex moduli.

Round each candidate's final endpoints outward to precision $p$. Return
success at the first stage where its radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$.
If relative tolerance was requested, set relative_certified to true exactly
when zero is excluded and the contract's relative-radius inequality holds;
failure of that relative test does not prevent absolute success. If no stage
produces a passing candidate, return inconclusive. The finite stage loop and
the finite elementary-range calls define the procedure completely.

derivations.claim: For $a=b=1,c=2$, the Pochhammer products give $(1)_k=k!$ and $(2)_k=(k+1)!$, so each coefficient is $1/(k+1)$. For $|z|<1$, the geometric series converges uniformly along the segment $sz$ ($0\le s\le1$). Parameterizing the path and integrating the real and imaginary component power series termwise by [F4] gives $$\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{z^{k+1}}{k+1} =\int_0^1\frac{z}{1-sz}\,ds=-\operatorname{Log}(1-z),$$ where [F2], [F3], and [F4] justify the path integral identity since $\operatorname{Re}(1-sz)>0$ along the segment. Dividing by $z$ gives the formula, and the series gives value $1$ at $z=0$.

The principal logarithm is holomorphic when $1-z$ avoids the nonpositive real axis, that is, when $z\notin[1,\infty)$. The quotient has a removable value at $z=0$ by step 1.1, so it defines the stated continuation domain, which contains $-2$.
Since $|-2|>1$, the defined Gauss-series branch fails its domain check and [F5] returns `domain`; this does not contradict the continued formula in step 2.1, which is a separately declared branch.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the exact output is $\operatorname{erfc}(x)$. Subtracting the perturbed inputs gives $$\widehat 1-\widehat{\operatorname{erf}} =\operatorname{erfc}(x)+\delta_1-\delta_2.$$ Since [F2] and [F3] give $\operatorname{erfc}(x)=2\pi^{-1/2}\int_x^\infty e^{-t^2}dt>0$, division by the exact value and the triangle inequality yield the stated relative-error bound.

The same tail integral tends to zero as $x\to\infty$, because the nonnegative Gaussian is integrable by [F3]. If $|\delta_1|,|\delta_2|\le\eta$ with fixed $\eta>0$, the choice $\delta_1=\eta$, $\delta_2=-\eta$ attains error $2\eta$, so the relative error is $2\eta/\operatorname{erfc}(x)$ and is unbounded. For an integer $n\ge0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, define

$$J_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}, \qquad I_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+n}}{k!(k+n)!}.$$

These are the integer-order Bessel and modified Bessel functions used on this
page. For real $x\ge0$, the scaled modified Bessel value means
$I_n^{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=e^{-x}I_n(x)$. This notation does not assert a finite
evaluation method or a truncation bound; those are proved separately.

For $n\ge0$ and either series in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]], the
absolute term ratio is

$$r_k=\frac{|z|^2}{4(k+1)(k+n+1)}.$$

The series for $J_n$ and $I_n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly in
$z\in\mathbb C$. If $K\ge0$ and
$q=|z|^2/[4(K+2)(K+n+2)]<1$, then the tail after terms $k=0,\ldots,K$ has
absolute value at most $|a_{K+1}|/(1-q)$, where $a_k$ is the corresponding
series term. The first two differentiated series also converge locally
uniformly.

For $z\ne0$, the functions in [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]] satisfy

$$z^2J_n''+zJ_n'+(z^2-n^2)J_n=0, \qquad z^2I_n''+zI_n'-(z^2+n^2)I_n=0.$$

For real or complex $z\ne0$ and integer $n\ge1$, they also satisfy

$$J_{n-1}(z)+J_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}J_n(z), \qquad I_{n-1}(z)-I_{n+1}(z)=\frac{2n}{z}I_n(z).$$

In addition, $J_0'(z)=-J_1(z)$.

At $z=0$, the series limits are $J_0(0)=I_0(0)=1$ and
$J_n(0)=I_n(0)=0$ for $n\ge1$.

Fix real $x>0$. Let $D_0(x)=-J_1(x)$ and $D_1(x)=J_0(x)$, and for every integer
$j\ge1$ define

$$D_{j+1}(x)=\frac{2j}{x}D_j(x)-D_{j-1}(x).$$

Thus $D$ is the second sequence obtained from the same order recurrence as
$J_j(x)$. It is a local auxiliary solution, not the Bessel function of the
second kind.

derivations.claim: Let $a_k=(1/2)^{2k+n}/(k!(k+n)!)$. By [F2], the positive terms $a_k$ decrease strictly to zero. Grouping the alternating series in consecutive pairs gives $J_n(1)=(a_0-a_1)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots>0$. Also $(k+n)!\ge n!$, so $$0<J_n(1)\le\sum_{k\ge0}a_k \le\frac{2^{-n}}{n!}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(1/4)^k}{k!} =\frac{2^{-n}e^{1/4}}{n!}\longrightarrow0.$$ In particular, $J_0(1)\ge1-1/4=3/4$ and $J_1(1)\ge1/2-1/16=7/16$.

By [F4], $D_0(1)=-J_1(1)<0$ and $D_1(1)=J_0(1)>0$; hence $D_2=2D_1-D_0>D_1>0$. If $n\ge2$ and $D_n\ge D_{n-1}>0$, then $D_{n+1}=2nD_n-D_{n-1}\ge(2n-1)D_n\ge3D_n$. Induction gives $D_n\ge3^{n-2}D_2$ for $n\ge2$, so $D_n\to\infty$.

The exact sequence $J_n-\varepsilon D_n$ obeys the same linear recurrence by [F3] and [F4], so it is the forward-recurrence solution from the displayed perturbed seeds. Since $J_n\to0$ and $D_n\to\infty$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, some finite $n$ satisfies $\varepsilon D_n>J_n$. At that index $\widetilde J_n<0<J_n$. The seed differences have magnitudes $\varepsilon|D_0|$ and $\varepsilon|D_1|$, which tend to zero with $\varepsilon$.

If the ratio of each term after a chosen first omitted term is bounded by
