A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

Whenever [[alg-certified-airy-evaluation]] returns `success`, its interval or
rectangle contains the requested $\operatorname{Ai}(z)$ or
$\operatorname{Bi}(z)$ and passes the requested absolute-radius test. Any
relative certificate is valid only when the enclosure excludes zero. No
success guarantee is made for every input or finite cap. Every execution with finite
caps terminates.

derivations.claim: At $x=\xi$, every enclosure containing the exact value also contains $0$. Therefore the zero-exclusion condition in [F3] fails, while [F4] still permits an absolute-radius success enclosure.

For any $\eta>0$, continuity in [F2] at the zero [F1] gives a neighborhood of $\xi$ on which $|\operatorname{Ai}(x)|<\eta$. Whenever a relative certificate succeeds for an enclosure $B$ of such a value, [F3] implies $\operatorname{rad}(B)\le\varepsilon_r d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r|\operatorname{Ai}(x)| <\varepsilon_r\eta$. Thus the required absolute radius tends to zero as the input approaches $\xi$.

$$J_n(x)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\cos(n\theta-x\sin\theta)\,d\theta, \qquad I_n(x)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi e^{x\cos\theta}\cos(n\theta)\,d\theta.$$

Consequently, for $x\ge0$,
$0\le e^{-x}I_n(x)\le1$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

Let $\sum a_n(x-c)^n$ have radius $R$, and let $[u,v]$ be a nonempty closed interval for which

$$r:=\max\{|u-c|,|v-c|\}<R.$$

Then the function series converges absolutely at every point of $[u,v]$ and converges uniformly there.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ne 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$
and put

$$q_k \;:=\; \Big|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\Big| \;=\; \frac{|a_{k+1}|}{|a_k|} \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}),$$

a genuine sequence on $\mathbb{N}$, whose limit superior and limit inferior exist
in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ for every such $(a_k)$ ([[lem-limsup-exists]]). Then:

1. if $\limsup_{k} q_k < 1$ then $\sum |a_k|$ converges, and hence $\sum a_k$
   converges as well ([[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]]);
2. if $\liminf_{k} q_k > 1$ then $\sum a_k$ diverges.

The hypothesis $a_k \ne 0$ is what makes $q_k$ exist and is not a convenience: a
single vanishing term leaves the ratio at that index undefined. For a family from
a starting index $m$ the statement is the one above applied to the shifted
sequence $j \mapsto a_{j+m}$ ([[def-series]]), whose ratios are
$|a_{j+m+1}/a_{j+m}|$.

**Nothing is claimed when $\limsup_k q_k \ge 1 \ge \liminf_k q_k$.** In that
regime the test is silent, and it has to be: the companion page carries a
convergent series whose ratios have limit superior $2$, and both a convergent and
a divergent series with ratio limit exactly $1$.

For every real $x$, both series
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$$
converge absolutely. Equivalently, both power series have infinite radius of convergence.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

The power-series sine and cosine satisfy the addition identities and
$\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$. For $A(t)=\arctan t$ from
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]],
$$
\sin(A(t))=t\cos(A(t)),\qquad \cos(A(t))>0,
$$
so $A(t)$ is the inverse tangent with values in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ when
$\pi=4A(1)$. It is odd; for $u,v\ge0$ with $uv<1$,
$A(u)+A(v)=A((u+v)/(1-uv))$; and for $t>0$,
$A(t)=\pi/2-A(1/t)$. In particular $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$. Also,
$$
\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239).
$$
For every real $x$ there is an integer $k$ and $r=x-k\pi/2$ with
$|r|\le\pi/4$; the sine and cosine of $x$ are obtained from those of $r$ by
the quarter-period identities. For every real $r$ with $|r|\le1$ and every
$N\ge0$, truncating sine
through degree $2N+1$ and cosine through degree $2N$ gives absolute tail bounds
$$
T_s=\frac{|r|^{2N+3}}{(2N+3)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+4)(2N+5)))}
$$
and
$$
T_c=\frac{|r|^{2N+2}}{(2N+2)!(1-|r|^2/((2N+3)(2N+4)))}.
$$

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

derivations.claim: Write $f_0(z)=\sin z/z$ and $g_0(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$. By [F2]–[F3], $f_0'=\cos z/z-\sin z/z^2$ and $f_0''=-\sin z/z-2\cos z/z^2+2\sin z/z^3$, so $L_0f_0=0$. Also $g_0'=e^{iz}(1/z+i/z^2)$ and $g_0''=e^{iz}(i/z-2/z^2-2i/z^3)$, so $L_0g_0=0$. For any function with the required finite derivatives on $(0,\infty)$, put $y_\ell=(-z)^\ell D^\ell f$ with $D=z^{-1}d/dz$. Since $(D^\ell f)'=zD^{\ell+1}f$, differentiating the product gives $y_\ell'=\ell y_\ell/z-y_{\ell+1}$, hence $y_{\ell+1}=\ell y_\ell/z-y_\ell'$. This recurrence applies to both functions in [F1].

The sine series gives $\sin z/z=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m z^{2m}/(2m+1)!$. After $r$ applications of $D$, the formal series is $\sum_{m\ge r}(-1)^m2^r m!z^{2m-2r}/((m-r)!(2m+1)!)$. For $z\ne0$ its successive nonzero absolute-term ratio is $|z|^2(m+1)/((m+1-r)(2m+2)(2m+3))\to0$; at $z=0$ only its constant term remains. Thus each such series has infinite radius by [F4]. Termwise differentiation and division by $z$ give the next series: the $m=r$ term is constant and differentiates to zero, so no negative power appears. The operation at $r=\ell$ kills $m<\ell$; its first remaining coefficient is $2^\ell\ell!/(2\ell+1)!=1/(2\ell+1)!!$ by [F9]. The later powers are $z^{\ell+2},z^{\ell+4},\ldots$; their coefficient series is bounded on $|z|\le1$ by compact uniform convergence in [F4], so their sum is $O(z^{\ell+2})$. This proves the stated origin expansion for $j_\ell$.

Put $\lambda=\ell(\ell+1)$ and $\mu=(\ell+1)(\ell+2)$. Direct differentiation gives $L_{\ell+1}(\ell y/z-y')=-y'''+(\ell-2)y''/z+(-1+\mu/z^2)y'+(\ell/z-\ell\mu/z^3)y=\ell L_\ell y/z-(L_\ell y)'$. Thus if $L_\ell y=0$, the recurrence in step 1.1 gives $L_{\ell+1}y_{\ell+1}=0$. Starting from step 1.1 proves both radial equations by induction. For $\ell\ge1$, differentiate $y_\ell=(\ell-1)y_{\ell-1}/z-y_{\ell-1}'$ and substitute $L_{\ell-1}y_{\ell-1}=0$; this yields $y_\ell'=(\ell+1)y_{\ell-1}'/z+(1-(\ell^2-1)/z^2)y_{\ell-1}$. Substituting $y_{\ell-1}'=(\ell-1)y_{\ell-1}/z-y_\ell$ from step 1.1 and collecting terms gives $y_\ell'=y_{\ell-1}-(\ell+1)y_\ell/z$.

Write $h_\ell^{(1)}=C_\ell e^{iz}$, starting with $C_0=-i/z$. Applying the recurrence of step 1.1 and the product rule in [F2]–[F3] gives $C_{\ell+1}=\ell C_\ell/z-C_\ell'-iC_\ell$. Induction shows $C_\ell$ is a finite Laurent polynomial with exponents $-1,\ldots,-\ell-1$. If its most singular term is $a_\ell z^{-\ell-1}$, the coefficient of $z^{-\ell-2}$ in $C_{\ell+1}$ is $(2\ell+1)a_\ell$; the term $-iC_\ell$ is less singular. Since $a_0=-i$, this gives $a_\ell=-i(2\ell-1)!!$. Also $e^{iz}=1+O(z)$ as $z\downarrow0$ by [F3] and differentiability at $0$, so the outgoing origin expansion follows. For infinity, induct on $\ell$ using step 1.1. The base terms are $j_0=\sin z/z$ and $h_0^{(1)}=-ie^{iz}/z$. If $j_\ell=\sin\theta/z+R_\ell$, $\theta=z-\ell\pi/2$, with $R_\ell$ a finite sum of $z^{-k}\sin z$ and $z^{-k}\cos z$ terms for $k\ge2$, then $R_\ell'=O(z^{-2})$ by [F3],[F7],[F8], and $\ell j_\ell/z=O(z^{-2})$; hence $j_{\ell+1}=-\cos\theta/z+O(z^{-2})=\sin(z-(\ell+1)\pi/2)/z+O(z^{-2})$ by the addition identities [F8]. For $h_\ell^{(1)}$, the coefficient recurrence gives a finite form $e^{iz}(b_\ell/z+\sum_{k=2}^{\ell+1}b_{\ell k}z^{-k})$. Its leading coefficient obeys $b_{\ell+1}=-ib_\ell$ because the terms $\ell C_\ell/z$ and $C_\ell'$ have powers at most $z^{-2}$; thus $b_\ell=(-i)^{\ell+1}$. The remainder and its derivative are $O(z^{-2})$ by [F3],[F7],[F8], so the recurrence gives $h_{\ell+1}^{(1)}=(-i)^{\ell+2}e^{iz}/z+O(z^{-2})$. Differentiating the leading terms and finite remainders also gives $j_\ell'=\cos(z-\ell\pi/2)/z+O(z^{-2})$ and $(h_\ell^{(1)})'=i(-i)^{\ell+1}e^{iz}/z+O(z^{-2})$.

For two solutions $y,v$ of $L_\ell y=0$, differentiation and substitution of their equations gives $(yv'-y'v)'=-2(yv'-y'v)/z$, hence $(z^2W[y,v])'=0$. Applying [F6] separately to the real and imaginary parts on $(0,\infty)$ shows $z^2W[j_\ell,h_\ell^{(1)}]$ is a constant complex number. With $\theta=z-\ell\pi/2$, the expansions and derivative expansions of step 2.2 give $z^2W[j_\ell,h_\ell^{(1)}]\longrightarrow(-i)^{\ell+1}e^{iz}(i\sin\theta-\cos\theta)=i$. Indeed, Euler's formula and the addition identities give $e^{iz}(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)=e^{i(z-\theta)}=e^{i\ell\pi/2}$; repeated use of $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ gives $e^{i\ell\pi/2}=i^\ell$. Since $i\sin\theta-\cos\theta=-(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)$ and $(-i)^{\ell+1}i^\ell=-i$, the displayed limit is $i$. The constant is therefore $i$, which proves the Wronskian formula.

for $r=0,\ldots,\ell-1$. With $s$ and $c$ denoting the sine and cosine input enclosures, form the unscaled outputs
$$u=A_\ell c+B_\ell s,\quad v=(A_\ell'+B_\ell)c+(B_\ell'-A_\ell)s,\quad w=C_\ell(c+is),\quad t=(C_\ell'+iC_\ell)(c+is).$$
Form the scaled outputs
$$c_\ell z^{-\ell}u,\quad c_\ell z^{-\ell}v,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}C_\ell,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}(C_\ell'+iC_\ell).$$
Collect like Laurent powers exactly; in particular cancel negative powers in the scaled $h_\ell^{(1)}$ value when they cancel algebraically. A remaining $z^{-1}$ in the scaled derivative is evaluated only on positive input intervals.

alg-certified-scaled-spherical-bessel-ev.finite_check_disposition: Hand-checked exact base-order graph identities; no software execution is claimed.

citations.quote:
For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $\ell\ge0$ be an integer and $z>0$ real. Put
$$c_\ell=(2\ell+1)!!=\prod_{r=0}^{\ell}(2r+1),\qquad d_\ell=(2\ell-1)!!=\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}(2r-1),$$
where the second product is empty and equals $1$ when $\ell=0$. Using the outgoing convention of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$J_\ell^{\rm sc}(z)=c_\ell z^{-\ell}j_\ell(z),\qquad D J_\ell^{\rm sc}(z)=c_\ell z^{-\ell}j_\ell'(z),$$
$$H_\ell^{\rm sc}(z)=d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}e^{-iz}h_\ell^{(1)}(z),\qquad D H_\ell^{\rm sc}(z)=d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}e^{-iz}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z).$$
The symbols $D J_\ell^{\rm sc}$ and $D H_\ell^{\rm sc}$ mean the scaled derivatives of the original functions, not derivatives of the scaled functions. The available targets are $j_\ell$, $j_\ell'$, $h_\ell^{(1)}$, $(h_\ell^{(1)})'$, and these four scaled quantities; every derivative is with respect to $z$.

An input is either (i) a closed dyadic interval $I=[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, requesting an enclosure of the whole target image on $I$, or (ii) a positive real $z$ supplied by an interface that, on each integer request $n\ge1$, terminates and returns a closed dyadic interval $I_n$ containing $z$ with width at most $2^{-n}$. The intervals need not be nested. This is a representation hypothesis on a supplied input, not a claim that every positive real has such a representation. An exact positive dyadic point is the constant-interface case $I_n=[z,z]$. A represented point need not be dyadic: arguments such as $kR$ or $\sqrt{k^2+V_0}R$ are admitted when a caller constructs a terminating interface by rigorous interval propagation from represented parameters. Each returned box must contain the exact composed argument; a midpoint or approximate point alone is not an admissible interface. The caller's construction must retain positivity and prove termination of every requested refinement.

For each target, outputs and optional relative tests use [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]: a real enclosure is an interval, a complex enclosure is a rectangle, and its radius is half its length or half its Euclidean diagonal, respectively. Each target has an exact positive rational absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a$; an exact positive rational relative tolerance $\varepsilon_r$ may also be requested. A relative flag may be true only when the returned enclosure excludes zero and $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$. No relative flag is available when the enclosure contains zero.

Intermediate interval endpoints may be exact rationals. Final endpoints are rounded outward to multiples of $2^{-p}$ for an integer $p\ge0$. The mathematical procedure has no fixed exponent limit. A concrete bounded implementation must return `range` or `inconclusive` rather than claim a finite result it cannot represent. Finite caps are specified by the evaluating algorithm. A fixed nondegenerate input interval requests its whole image and is not promised arbitrarily small radius; eventual absolute success is asserted separately for represented-point inputs.

Inputs are those of [[def-spherical-bessel-evaluation-contract]], a nonempty finite list of valid targets, finite exact positive rational absolute tolerances, optional exact positive rational relative tolerances, and finite integer caps $W,Q,M_{\max},p_{\max}\ge1$. $W$ is the maximum exact-arithmetic work count, $Q$ the maximum stage and represented-point interface index, $M_{\max}$ the maximum Taylor degree, and $p_{\max}$ the maximum final dyadic precision. A Gaussian rational is $a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. A Laurent polynomial is a finite sum $\sum_k a_k z^k$ with integer exponents and Gaussian-rational coefficients; its formal derivative uses $(z^k)'=kz^{k-1}$. An expression graph below is a finite directed acyclic graph of exact rational arithmetic operations.

Factorials are those of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]; they are nonzero by that definition and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]], so every displayed factorial denominator is defined. For a rational $x$, $\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the least integer greater than or equal to $x$, computed by exact integer division.

Reject an invalid order, target, tolerance, cap, or interval input not contained in $(0,\infty)$ with `domain`. For a represented point, an interval returned by the input interface may meet zero; such a stage is skipped and a later interface index is tried.

Construct Laurent polynomials by
$$A_0=0,\quad B_0=z^{-1},\quad C_0=-iz^{-1},$$
$$A_{r+1}=rz^{-1}A_r-A_r'-B_r,\quad B_{r+1}=rz^{-1}B_r-B_r'+A_r,\quad C_{r+1}=rz^{-1}C_r-C_r'-iC_r$$
for $r=0,\ldots,\ell-1$. With $s$ and $c$ denoting the sine and cosine input enclosures, form the unscaled outputs
$$u=A_\ell c+B_\ell s,\quad v=(A_\ell'+B_\ell)c+(B_\ell'-A_\ell)s,\quad w=C_\ell(c+is),\quad t=(C_\ell'+iC_\ell)(c+is).$$
Form the scaled outputs
$$c_\ell z^{-\ell}u,\quad c_\ell z^{-\ell}v,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}C_\ell,\quad d_\ell^{-1}z^{\ell+1}(C_\ell'+iC_\ell).$$
Collect like Laurent powers exactly; in particular cancel negative powers in the scaled $h_\ell^{(1)}$ value when they cancel algebraically. A remaining $z^{-1}$ in the scaled derivative is evaluated only on positive input intervals.

For real intervals use exact rational endpoint hulls: $[a,b]+[c,d]=[a+c,b+d]$, $[a,b][c,d]=[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$, and $[a,b]^{-1}=[1/b,1/a]$ when $0<a\le b$. For complex rectangles, apply these real interval operations to the real and imaginary components of $(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. Thus interval arithmetic encloses every pointwise sum and product; division is only by a positive power of the positive argument or by a positive integer constant. Compute powers, factorials, and rational endpoints by finite exact arithmetic.

At a positive current box $I=[a,b]$, choose $M\ge0$ with $M+2\ge2b$ and form the rational interval polynomial and rational tail
$$T_M(I)=\sum_{m=0}^{M}\frac{(iI)^m}{m!},\qquad E_M=\frac{2b^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}.$$
The interval power is repeated complex-rectangle multiplication. Enclose $\cos(I)$ by $\operatorname{Re}T_M(I)+[-E_M,E_M]$ and $\sin(I)$ by $\operatorname{Im}T_M(I)+[-E_M,E_M]$. Evaluate each requested output graph with these leaves and $z\in I$, and round each final endpoint outward to the grid $2^{-p}\mathbb Z$.

Use the following deterministic finite search. Charge the Laurent recurrence, graph construction, and coefficient collection to the work counter as they are performed. For stages $q=1,\ldots,Q$, first take the fixed interval unchanged, or call the represented-point interface at index $q$. Skip a represented-point stage unless its returned interval has $a>0$. Set $p=q$ and $M=\max(q,\lceil2b\rceil)$. If $p>p_{\max}$ or $M>M_{\max}$, stop with `inconclusive`. Evaluate all requested graphs and the displayed $T_M,E_M$ using the work counter: each exact rational or Gaussian-rational arithmetic operation or comparison, each Taylor term, each endpoint-rounding operation, and each interface call costs one unit. If the next operation would exceed $W$, stop with `inconclusive` before performing it. If the output format cannot represent a certified endpoint, return `range` with no finite claim. If every requested target has radius at most its absolute tolerance, return `success`; for each optional relative tolerance, set its flag true exactly when the enclosure excludes zero and the relative test in the contract passes. A failed relative test does not prevent absolute `success`. If no stage succeeds before a cap or the search ends, return `inconclusive`. No floating-point recurrence is used.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

If $\sum a_n=A$ and $\sum b_n=B$ converge absolutely in $\mathbb C$, and $c_n=\sum_{k\le n}a_kb_{n-k}$, then $\sum c_n$ converges absolutely and has sum $AB$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-absolute-convergence-of-complex-series]], [[thm-complex-plane-is-complete]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[def-monoid-finite-product]], [[thm-generalised-associativity]], [[cor-cauchy-product-absolute]], [[thm-direct-comparison-test]], [[lem-series-linearity]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]].

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ne 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$
and put

$$q_k \;:=\; \Big|\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}\Big| \;=\; \frac{|a_{k+1}|}{|a_k|} \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}),$$

a genuine sequence on $\mathbb{N}$, whose limit superior and limit inferior exist
in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ for every such $(a_k)$ ([[lem-limsup-exists]]). Then:

1. if $\limsup_{k} q_k < 1$ then $\sum |a_k|$ converges, and hence $\sum a_k$
   converges as well ([[lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence]]);
2. if $\liminf_{k} q_k > 1$ then $\sum a_k$ diverges.

The hypothesis $a_k \ne 0$ is what makes $q_k$ exist and is not a convenience: a
single vanishing term leaves the ratio at that index undefined. For a family from
a starting index $m$ the statement is the one above applied to the shifted
sequence $j \mapsto a_{j+m}$ ([[def-series]]), whose ratios are
$|a_{j+m+1}/a_{j+m}|$.

**Nothing is claimed when $\limsup_k q_k \ge 1 \ge \liminf_k q_k$.** In that
regime the test is silent, and it has to be: the companion page carries a
convergent series whose ratios have limit superior $2$, and both a convergent and
a divergent series with ratio limit exactly $1$.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

derivations.claim: For $y_\ell=(-z)^\ell D^\ell f$, differentiation as in [F1] gives $y_{\ell+1}=\ell y_\ell/z-y_\ell'$. Starting from $j_0=\sin z/z=A_0\cos z+B_0\sin z$ with $A_0=0,B_0=z^{-1}$, the derivative formula $(A_\ell\cos z+B_\ell\sin z)'=(A_\ell'+B_\ell)\cos z+(B_\ell'-A_\ell)\sin z$ gives exactly the algorithm's $A_{\ell+1},B_{\ell+1}$. Starting from $h_0^{(1)}=-ie^{iz}/z=C_0e^{iz}$ with $C_0=-i/z$, the componentwise product rule [F5]–[F6] gives $(C_\ell e^{iz})'=(C_\ell'+iC_\ell)e^{iz}$ and exactly the algorithm's recurrence for $C_{\ell+1}$. Euler's identity [F6] identifies the algorithm's $c+is$ with $e^{iz}$. Thus $u,v,w,t$ represent $j_\ell,j_\ell',h_\ell^{(1)},(h_\ell^{(1)})'$, respectively.

The two series for $e^{-iz}$ and $e^{iz}$ are absolutely convergent by [F2], so [F7] identifies their product with the sum of the Cauchy-product coefficients. For total degree $n$, its coefficient is $z^n S_n$, where $S_n=\sum_{r=0}^{n}(-i)^r i^{n-r}/(r!(n-r)!)$. For $1\le r\le n$, combining over the denominator $r!(n+1-r)!$ and using $(n+1-r)!=(n+1-r)(n-r)!$ and $r!=r(r-1)!$ gives $1/(r!(n+1-r)!)=(1/(n+1))(1/(r!(n-r)!)+1/((r-1)!(n+1-r)!))$. For $r=0$ or $r=n+1$, omit the summand whose index is outside $0,\ldots,n$; the remaining summand equals the left side by $0!=1$. Splitting the finite sum for $S_{n+1}$ with this identity and reindexing its second part gives $S_{n+1}=(iS_n-iS_n)/(n+1)=0$ for every $n\ge0$, while $S_0=1$. The factorials and $n+1$ are nonzero by [F2], so these divisions are defined. Hence the product series has constant coefficient $1$ and every positive-degree coefficient $0$, so $e^{-iz}e^{iz}=1$.

Fix a positive input box $I=[a,b]$ and choose $M$ with $M+2\ge2b$. For every $z\in I$, the first omitted absolute exponential-series term is at most $b^{M+1}/(M+1)!$. Each subsequent ratio is at most $b/(M+2)\le1/2$, so the sum of the omitted terms is at most $2b^{M+1}/(M+1)!=E_M$. Thus the real and imaginary parts of $T_M(z)$, enlarged by $[-E_M,E_M]$, contain $\cos z$ and $\sin z$. Exact rational interval addition and multiplication enclose pointwise addition and multiplication by their endpoint-hull formulas; inversion of a positive interval $[a,b]$ is $[1/b,1/a]$. Evaluation over the finite graph and outward rounding therefore preserve containment of every graph value on $I$.

Each cap bounds its corresponding loop or finite expansion. The Laurent graph for fixed $\ell$ is finite; each rational operation and each terminating represented-point interface call takes finite work, and every cap exhaustion has an explicit status return. Therefore every capped execution terminates, including one that never obtains a positive point box or never passes its requested tests.

Fix a positive represented point $z_0$. By [F10], choose a sufficiently large index $q_0$ that $2^{-q_0}<z_0/4$. Write $I_{q_0}=[a_0,b_0]$; the interface width bound gives $a_0>0$. For all $q\ge q_0$, $I_q\subset[a_0/2,b_0+1]=:[a,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, because $I_q$ contains $z_0$, has width at most $2^{-q_0}$, and $z_0-2^{-q_0}>a_0/2$ while $z_0+2^{-q_0}<b_0+1$. Thus $M=q$ eventually and $E_M\le2B^{q+1}/(q+1)!\to0$, since the successive ratios are eventually at most $1/2$. Put $\delta_q=\operatorname{width}(I_q)$. For $m\ge1$, positivity of $I_q=[a_q,b_q]$ makes repeated complex-rectangle multiplication of $iI_q$ exact along one coordinate: its $m$th power is $i^m[a_q^m,b_q^m]$ up to the sign absorbed by the interval endpoints. Therefore $\operatorname{width}(I_q^m)=b_q^m-a_q^m\le mB^{m-1}\delta_q$ by factoring the difference of powers. Each degree-$m$ term in $T_M(I_q)$ has component width at most $\delta_qB^{m-1}/(m-1)!$, so each component of the polynomial interval has width at most $\delta_q\sum_{m=1}^{M}B^{m-1}/(m-1)!$. The terms of the last series are nonzero because $B>0$, and their successive ratio is $B/m\to0$; [F8] makes its sum finite, say $C_B$. With the Taylor tail added, the sine and cosine enclosure widths tend to zero.

Multiplying the unscaled expressions of step 1.1 by the scales in [[def-spherical-bessel-evaluation-contract]] gives the four scaled identities. For $H_\ell^{\rm sc}$ and $D H_\ell^{\rm sc}$, cancel $e^{-iz}e^{iz}$ by step 1.2; the derivative scale acts on the original $h_\ell^{(1)}$ derivative as defined, not on $H_\ell^{\rm sc}$. Starting with $C_0=-iz^{-1}$, if $C_\ell$ has exponents $-1,\ldots,-\ell-1$, then $\ell z^{-1}C_\ell$ and $C_\ell'$ have exponents at least $-\ell-2$, while $-iC_\ell$ has exponents at least $-\ell-1$; induction gives only exponents $-1,\ldots,-\ell-1$ in $C_\ell$. Thus $z^{\ell+1}C_\ell$ is a polynomial and $z^{\ell+1}(C_\ell'+iC_\ell)$ has at worst exponent $-1$, which is well-defined on the positive input domain.

The remaining expression graph is fixed and finite. On $[a,B]$, each reciprocal has width $\delta_q/(a_qb_q)\le\delta_q/a^2$ and is bounded. Sums of bounded intervals with widths tending to zero also have widths tending to zero; for bounded real intervals $X,Y$, $\operatorname{width}(XY)\le\sup|X|\operatorname{width}(Y)+\sup|Y|\operatorname{width}(X)$. Applying these bounds to the real component operations in each complex rectangle proves by induction that every output rectangle or interval has width tending to zero. By [F10], the outward rounding increment $2^{1-q}$ also tends to zero, so all output radii tend to zero. Thus every positive rational absolute tolerance is passed at some finite stage, and the finite work through that stage gives finite sufficient caps. Constant interfaces prove the exact positive-dyadic case as well.

By steps 1.1 and 2.1 the graph roots are the exact requested targets. Step 1.3 encloses the sine and cosine leaves for every admissible argument; induction through the finite graph, using the interval formulas in [F4], encloses every sum, product, reciprocal, and requested output value. Outward endpoint rounding preserves these containments. The success-radius and relative-flag tests are precisely the contract in [F9], so every finite success is sound for point or whole-interval input.

If a requested target has value $v\ne0$, any sound enclosure $B$ of step 3.1 has diameter $2\operatorname{rad}(B)$ and contains $v$, so $d(B,0)\ge |v|-2\operatorname{rad}(B)$. Eventually $d(B,0)\ge|v|/2>0$ and $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\to0$, giving any requested positive rational relative tolerance along the refined sequence. The algorithm may already have stopped with absolute success before that relative test passes. To obtain the relative flag, rerun with successively smaller positive rational absolute tolerances and increasing finite caps: step 2.2 supplies a successful finite capped run for each such tolerance, and its returned radius is bounded by that tolerance. For a finite list of nonzero requested targets, sufficiently small absolute tolerances make all requested relative flags true. If $v=0$, every sound enclosure contains zero and no relative flag is available. A fixed interval input encloses its whole image, which may have positive diameter, so the point-mode limiting argument asserts no arbitrary-radius guarantee there.
